one: Short documents recording one significant decision: context, options, the choice, and its consequences.
an: Ship's log entries. Months later, anyone can see why the captain changed course, not just that the ship is somewhere new.
how: Template: Title, Status (proposed / accepted / rejected / deprecated / superseded), Context (forces and constraints), Decision, Consequences (good and bad), Alternatives considered.
One page. Stored in the repo (docs/adr/0007-use-postgres-for-search.md), reviewed like code.
Superseded, never deleted: the history of reasoning is the value.
why: "Why on earth did we pick X?" is answered in minutes instead of archaeology. New hires learn the system's reasoning. Prevents re-litigating settled decisions.
trade: Only for decisions that are costly to reverse. Recording every small choice turns it into bureaucracy.

myth.r: A 20-minute ADR saves hours of repeated debate and protects against reversing a decision whose reason was forgotten.

q.s: Which is the most important part of an ADR for someone reading it 2 years later?
o: The author's name
The context and constraints at the time, plus alternatives rejected
The date only
The diagram colours
q.e: Without context, the decision looks arbitrary and gets reversed for the wrong reasons.

more: When a decision deserves an ADR
lab: Write three ADRs for decisions already made in one of your projects (e.g. database choice, hosting, auth provider). Include the alternatives you rejected.

plain:
An Architecture Decision Record is a short document (about one page) recording one important decision: the situation, the options considered, what was chosen, and the consequences. It lives in the repo next to the code.

Months later, anyone can see why things are the way they are.
bridge: It is a good PR description for a decision instead of a code change: context, alternatives, trade-offs, chosen path.

walk.title: Writing ADR 0015: payments provider
steps: Context: we need card payments in Uzbekistan; Payme and Click fees are higher than expected; Octo offers 0.8%.
Options: Payme + Click, Octo, build on a bank's acquiring API directly.
Decision: Octo, because of fees and one integration covering Uzcard and Humo.
Consequences: one vendor dependency; we wrap it in an adapter so switching is possible; we must handle their webhook format.
A year later a new developer asks “why Octo?” and reads it in two minutes instead of interrupting three people.

terms: The forces and constraints at decision time.
What becomes easier or harder because of the decision.
Replaced by a newer decision (keep the old one for history).
insights: Keep an index file (number, title, status). Once there are 30+ ADRs, people search the index, not the folder.
Write assumptions as checkable facts (“under 2M documents”, “one region”), so anyone can see when an ADR needs revisiting.
When a PR goes against an accepted ADR, link it and ask “what changed?” instead of arguing from scratch.

prod.summary: In real teams an ADR is a short Markdown file in the repo, reviewed in a normal pull request, numbered in order, and never edited after it is accepted, only superseded. Seniors care less about the template and more about two things: that the hard-to-reverse decisions actually get recorded, and that the context section would still make sense to someone who joins in two years.
checklist: The decision is costly to reverse (database, auth provider, sync vs async, monorepo, a public API shape). Small, cheap-to-change choices do not need an ADR.
Context names the real constraints with numbers: traffic, team size, budget, deadline, regulation (“data must stay in-country”).
At least two real alternatives are listed with the reason each lost, including “do nothing”.
Consequences include the bad ones: new operational work, lock-in, things that become harder.
Status is set (proposed, accepted, deprecated, superseded by ADR-NNNN) and the old ADR links to the new one when replaced.
The ADR is merged through a PR, so the people affected had a chance to comment, and code that depends on it links to it in a comment.
Someone owns revisiting it if a stated assumption changes (e.g. “we stay under 1M rows”).
numbers: Michael Nygard's original 2011 format has five parts: Title, Context, Decision, Status, Consequences.

MADR 4.0.0 (September 2024) adds Decision Drivers, Considered Options, Pros and Cons of the Options and Confirmation; its status values include proposed, rejected, accepted, deprecated and “superseded by ADR-NNNN”.
failures: A new engineer opens a PR to “switch from Postgres full-text search to Elasticsearch, it is obviously better”, and the team has the same two-hour debate as last year.

The original decision was made in a meeting and never written down. Write the ADR now (even late), with the constraints that drove it (one less system to run, under 2M documents). Next time, link the ADR in the PR thread and the debate becomes “has the context changed?”.
The docs/adr folder has 140 files, most about lint rules and folder names, and nobody reads it.
ADRs were used for every small choice, so the important ones are buried. Move conventions to a contributing guide; keep ADRs for hard-to-reverse decisions; add an index file with status per ADR.
An accepted ADR says “we use Redis for sessions”, but the code moved to signed cookies a year ago. Readers trust the ADR and are misled.
The decision changed without a new ADR. Add a rule in the PR template: “Does this change an accepted ADR? Link the superseding ADR.” Mark the old one “Superseded by ADR-0031”.
An ADR reads “Decision: use Kafka. Reason: it is scalable.” Two years later nobody can tell if it still applies.

No context and no rejected alternatives. Rewrite it with the numbers at decision time (events per second, retention needs) and what was rejected (SQS, Postgres outbox), so a future reader can check whether the forces still hold.

code.title: A complete one-page ADR (Nygard format plus alternatives)
code.src:
# ADR-0007: Use PostgreSQL full-text search instead of Elasticsearch

Status: Accepted (2026-03-12)
Deciders: backend team, tech lead

## Context
- Product search over ~400k listings, growing ~10k/month.
- p95 search latency target: 300 ms.
- Team of 4 backend engineers; nobody has run Elasticsearch in production.
- We already run PostgreSQL 17 with daily backups and on-call coverage.

## Decision
Use PostgreSQL full-text search (tsvector + GIN index) with pg_trgm
for typo tolerance. No new datastore.

## Alternatives considered
- Elasticsearch / OpenSearch: better relevance tuning, but a new cluster
  to run, sync pipeline to build, and a second source of truth.
- Managed search SaaS: fastest to ship, but ~$300/month at our size
  and listing data leaves our region.

## Consequences
+ No new infrastructure, no sync lag, transactional consistency.
- Relevance tuning is limited; facets need hand-written SQL.
- Revisit if listings exceed ~5M or p95 goes above 300 ms
  (owner: search squad, checked each quarter).
code.note: The last line is the most useful part: it states the assumption that would make this decision wrong, so the team knows when to write ADR-00NN to supersede it.

qs.s: Your team decided last week to move from REST to GraphQL for the mobile API. Another lead says “just put it in the Slack channel, ADRs are overhead.” What is the strongest argument for an ADR here?
o: Slack messages are hard to search, and an ADR in the repo keeps the context and rejected options next to the code, for people who join after the discussion
ADRs are required by most compliance standards
ADRs make the decision impossible to change later
An ADR gives the decision an author who can be blamed if it fails
qs.e: The value is durable context for future readers, stored where they will look. ADRs do not lock decisions (they can be superseded), and blame is the opposite of the goal. Compliance rarely requires ADRs specifically.

qs.s: ADR-0012 (accepted 2024) says “Use a single Postgres database for all services.” Now one service needs 10x the write throughput and you decide to give it its own database. What do you do with ADR-0012?
o: Edit ADR-0012 to describe the new design
Delete ADR-0012 so nobody is confused
Write ADR-0038 explaining the new context and decision, and mark ADR-0012 “Superseded by ADR-0038”
Leave ADR-0012 unchanged and mention the change in the release notes
qs.e: Accepted ADRs are not rewritten: the old reasoning is history that explains why the system looked the way it did. A new ADR records the new context, and the status link lets readers follow the chain. Leaving it unchanged makes the repo lie.

qs.s: Which of these decisions most clearly deserves an ADR?
o: Choosing to store money as integer minor units (tiyin/cents) instead of floats across all services
Renaming utils.ts to helpers.ts
Adding a new ESLint rule for import order
Picking a colour for the error toast
qs.e: Money representation touches the database, every API and every report, and is very costly to reverse after data exists. The others are cheap to change and belong in conventions or code review, not ADRs.

qs.s: Read this ADR, merged last year. A new engineer now wants to replace Kafka with SQS. What is the biggest problem with the ADR?

code.title: docs/adr/0011-use-kafka.md
code.src:
# ADR-0011: Use Kafka for events

Status: Accepted

## Context
We need a message queue between services.

## Decision
Use Kafka. It is the industry standard and it scales.

## Consequences
Services publish events to Kafka.

o: It should be stored in Confluence, not in the repo
It is too short; ADRs should be at least three pages
The context has no real constraints (volume, ordering, retention, team skills) and no rejected options or costs, so nobody can tell if the reasons still hold
It does not name the engineer who wrote it
qs.e: An ADR is useful when a future reader can check whether the forces behind it still exist. “Industry standard, it scales” cannot be checked, and there is no cost listed (running a Kafka cluster). Length is not the issue; one page with numbers is enough. The storage location and author name do not help the decision.

qs.s: A teammate opens a PR that edits the Decision section of accepted ADR-0009 from “REST between services” to “gRPC between services”, because the team switched last month. What is the right review comment?
o: Ask for a new ADR that explains the new context and decision, and change only the status line of ADR-0009 to “Superseded by ADR-00NN”
Approve: the ADR should always match the current code
Reject the PR; accepted ADRs can never change, even the status
Ask them to delete ADR-0009 and keep only the new decision
qs.e: Editing the old decision erases why REST was chosen and why that changed. The accepted record stays as history; only its status line is updated to point at the replacement. “Never touch it” is too strict: the status must change, or readers trust an outdated decision.

qs.s: Your repo has ADR-0004 “Single PostgreSQL datastore for all services” (context: team of 5, under 1M rows per table). You review this PR. What is the best lead response?

code.title: PR #812: add Mongo for the activity feed
code.src:
docker-compose.yml
+  mongo:
+    image: mongo:8
+    ports: ["27017:27017"]

package.json
+    "mongodb": "^6.10.0",

src/feed/store.ts
+ // Mongo is better for feeds
+ export const feed = client.db("app").collection("feed");

o: Approve; the author knows the feed best
Block it permanently because ADR-0004 forbids a second database
Ask the author to remove the code comment and then approve
Link ADR-0004 and ask what changed in its context (data size, access pattern, team). If the case is real, write an ADR that supersedes or narrows ADR-0004 before merging
qs.e: A new datastore is a hard-to-reverse decision (backups, on-call, monitoring, skills). The ADR makes the review a focused question: has the context changed? An ADR is not a permanent ban; it can be superseded with good reasons. Approving silently makes ADR-0004 lie.

qs.s: Your team writes ADRs only after the work is finished, “for documentation”. What does the team lose by doing this?
o: Nothing; the content is the same whenever you write it
The review step: people affected cannot comment on a “proposed” decision before code exists, and rejected options are often forgotten by the time it is written
Legal protection, because ADRs written later are not valid
The ADR number order, which must match the commit order
qs.e: The ADR is most valuable as a proposal reviewed in a PR: other teams can raise problems while the decision is still cheap to change. Written afterwards, it often justifies the result and misses the alternatives. A late ADR is still better than none, which is why “nothing lost” is tempting but wrong.

interview.q: How do you decide which decisions deserve an ADR?
answer: The main test is the cost to reverse: datastores, auth, sync vs async communication, public API shape, money representation, hosting model.
Also decisions that cross team boundaries, or that people keep debating.
Not for cheap choices (lint rules, folder names): those go in a contributing guide or code review, otherwise the important ADRs get buried.
Write it as “proposed” in a PR before building, so the affected people can review it.
Include a revisit trigger: the assumption that would make the decision wrong.
followups: Give an example of a decision you recorded that was later superseded.
How do you stop the ADR folder from becoming unread?

interview.q: Walk me through what goes into a good ADR.
answer: Title as a decision (“Use Postgres full-text search”), status, date and deciders.
Context with real numbers and constraints: load, data size, team skills, budget, regulation.
At least two real alternatives, including “do nothing”, and why each lost.
Consequences, including the bad ones: new operational work, lock-in, what gets harder.
Format: Nygard's five parts or MADR; the template matters less than honest context.
followups: What do you do when the team cannot agree on the decision?
How is an ADR different from a design doc?

interview.q: An ADR from two years ago no longer matches the system. What do you do?
answer: Find out when and why the system changed; often it was a decision made in code without a record.
Write a new ADR with today's context and decision, and mark the old one “Superseded by ADR-NNNN”. Do not rewrite or delete the old one.
Check code comments and docs that link to the old ADR.
Add a PR template question (“Does this change an accepted ADR?”) so it does not happen again.
followups: Why not simply edit the old ADR?
Who owns keeping ADRs current?

diagrams.title: ADR status lifecycle
diagrams.src:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Proposed: PR opened
  Proposed --> Accepted: PR merged
  Proposed --> Rejected: team says no
  Accepted --> Deprecated: no longer applies
  Accepted --> Superseded: new ADR replaces it

codeCheck.detail: A written ADR, not code; no numbers to check. Dates and versions reviewed by hand.

videos.t: Architecture Decision Records (ADR) as a LOG that answers "WHY?"
videos.why: ADRs as a log that answers why.
Mark Richards on the structure of a good ADR.

one: A written proposal for a significant piece of work, circulated for feedback before building.
an: An architect's drawings reviewed before pouring concrete. Changing a line on paper costs nothing; moving a wall later costs a lot.
how: Sections: problem and goals (and non-goals), background, proposed design, alternatives with trade-offs, data model and APIs, rollout and migration plan, risks, observability, open questions, cost estimate.
Write for a reader who was not in the meeting. Diagrams for flows, numbers for scale (see estimation).
Review asynchronously, then a short meeting only for open disagreements.
why: Writing forces clarity; review spreads knowledge and catches expensive mistakes early. Senior and lead promotions often hinge on this skill.
trade: Doc length should match risk. A two-day change needs a paragraph; a migration of the billing system needs a real document.

myth.r: Agile means no big upfront design. A few pages of thinking before weeks of building is cheap risk reduction.

q.s: Which section most often prevents scope creep in a design doc?
o: Background
Explicit non-goals
Appendix
Glossary
q.e: Writing down what you will not do stops the project silently growing during review and build.

lab: Write a 2-page design doc for a real upcoming feature: problem, goals, non-goals, design, alternatives, rollout, risks. Ask one person to review it in comments.
docs: Malte Ubl: Design docs at Google
Gergely Orosz: RFCs and design docs

plain:
A design doc is a written plan for a significant piece of work, shared for feedback before building. It describes the problem, goals and non-goals, the proposed design, the alternatives, and the risks.

Changing a plan in a document costs minutes. Changing a built system costs weeks.
bridge: If you have ever built a feature for two weeks and then heard “that's not what we meant”, a one-page design doc shared on day one would have caught it.

walk.title: A two-page doc for “team invitations”
steps: Problem: customers want to invite colleagues; today they share one login.
Goals: invite by email, roles (admin/member), revoke. Non-goals: SSO, custom roles (later).
Design: invitations table, signed expiring links, email via the existing queue, UI in settings. A small sequence diagram.
Alternatives: magic-link only accounts (rejected: breaks existing password login).
Rollout: behind a flag, enable for 3 customers first. Reviewers spot a missing case (invite an email that already has an account) before any code exists.

terms: A written proposal reviewed before implementation.
What the project explicitly will not do.
Other options and why they lost.
How the change reaches users safely.
insights: Put the one hard question at the top. Reviewers give their best attention to the first page.
Each non-goal is a debate you will not have in the middle of building.
After building, add a short “what changed from the doc” note, so the doc does not mislead the next reader.

prod.summary: In production teams a design doc (often called an RFC) is written before work that is risky, cross-team, or longer than a couple of weeks. It is reviewed asynchronously in comments by the people who will build, run and depend on the system. Seniors judge a doc by whether it names the hard part, the non-goals, the rollout and rollback plan, and how you will know it works in production.
checklist: The first paragraph states the problem and why now, in terms a reader outside the team understands.
Goals are measurable (“p95 checkout under 800 ms”, “zero downtime during migration”); non-goals are explicit.
At least two alternatives are compared honestly, including the simplest one.
Data model and API changes are shown concretely (table definitions, request/response examples), with backwards compatibility addressed.
Rollout plan: feature flag, percentage rollout, migration steps, and a tested rollback path for each step.
Observability: which metrics, logs and alerts will show the change is healthy, with thresholds.
Reviewers include the owners of every system it touches (on-call, security, data, the consuming team), with a review deadline.
numbers: Google's design docs are typically 10–20 pages for large projects; a “mini design doc” of 1–3 pages is used for smaller changes (Malte Ubl, “Design Docs at Google”).
A common practice is a fixed review window (for example one week) and a named approver, so a doc does not sit open for a month.
Rule of thumb used by many teams: write a doc when work is over ~2 engineer-weeks, touches another team's system, or changes a data model that stores customer data.
failures: The doc has 60 comments after three weeks, no decision, and the team started building anyway.
No decider and no deadline. Name one approver and a review end date in the header. Resolve the remaining disagreements in one 30-minute meeting, then record the outcome in the doc (or an ADR).
Halfway through the migration, the team discovers the old and new schemas cannot run side by side, so rollback means data loss.
The rollout section said “deploy and migrate” without steps. Require an expand–migrate–contract plan with a rollback for each step, and have someone who runs the database review it.
The feature ships, then the support team is surprised by new error emails and the data team's dashboards break.
Affected stakeholders were not reviewers. Add a “Who is affected” section and tag those teams; give them the same review deadline.
The doc is 25 pages and reviewers only comment on typos in the first section.
Length did not match risk, and the key decision was hidden. Put a one-paragraph summary and the main open question at the top; move background to an appendix.

code.title: A design doc skeleton that real reviewers can work with
code.src:
Title: Team invitations
Author: A. Karimov   Reviewers: backend, security, support
Approver: tech lead   Review closes: 2026-10-14   Status: In review

1. Summary (5 lines): what we build and the one decision we need.
2. Problem and why now: customers share one login; 18 support
   tickets/month ask for multi-user access.
3. Goals: invite by email, admin/member roles, revoke access.
   Success: 30% of paying teams have 2+ members within 60 days.
4. Non-goals: SSO, custom roles, invites across organisations.
5. Proposed design: invitations table, signed links expiring in
   7 days, email via existing queue. Sequence diagram.
6. API and data model: endpoints with example payloads; migration.
7. Alternatives: (a) magic-link-only accounts, (b) do nothing.
8. Security and privacy: link guessing, revoked users' sessions.
9. Rollout: flag on for 3 customers, then 25%, then 100%.
   Rollback: turn flag off; table stays, unused.
10. Observability: invite_sent, invite_accepted, accept errors;
    alert if accept error rate > 2% for 15 min.
11. Open questions: what if the email already has an account?
code.note: The header lines (approver and review close date) prevent the most common failure: a doc that is discussed forever and decided never.

qs.s: A design doc for moving file uploads from your servers to direct-to-S3 uploads has a strong design section but the rollout section says only “deploy behind a flag”. What is the most important thing to ask for in review?
o: A more detailed architecture diagram
What happens to uploads in progress and existing files during the switch, and how to roll back without losing files
A comparison with Google Cloud Storage
A longer background section about S3
qs.e: The risk in this change is the transition: in-flight uploads, old file URLs and rollback. A flag alone does not answer what happens to data written while the flag was on. Diagrams and vendor comparisons do not reduce that risk.

qs.s: Your doc has been in review for 4 weeks. Two senior engineers disagree about using a queue vs synchronous calls, and each new comment restarts the debate. What should you do as the author?
o: Wait until they agree in the comments
Remove the section so the doc can be approved
Start building with your preferred option and update the doc later
Write both options with their trade-offs in the doc, hold a short meeting with the named approver, and record the decision and reasoning
qs.e: Async review is good for finding issues but bad at ending deadlocks. A decider plus a short meeting closes it, and recording the reasoning keeps the doc useful. Building first ignores reviewers; deleting the section hides the key decision.

qs.s: Which work most clearly needs a full design doc rather than a short PR description?
o: Changing how the billing service calculates proration, used by 3 other teams and stored in invoices
Adding a new field to a settings form
Upgrading a UI library minor version
Fixing a typo in an error message
qs.e: It touches money, other teams and stored data, so mistakes are expensive and visible to customers. The others are small, local and easy to reverse.

qs.s: These are the goals in a design doc for a checkout rewrite. Which rewrite of the goals is best?

code.title: Design doc: Checkout v2, section 3
code.src:
3. Goals
- Make checkout faster.
- Improve reliability.
- Better code quality.

4. Non-goals
(none)

o: Keep them; goals should stay general so the team has freedom
“p95 checkout API latency under 800 ms (today 2.1 s); payment error rate under 0.5% (today 1.8%)”, plus non-goals such as “no new payment methods, no UI redesign”
Add more goals so reviewers see the full value
Move the goals to the end of the doc
qs.e: Measurable goals with today's baseline let reviewers judge the design and let you prove success after launch. Non-goals stop scope creep during review. General goals feel flexible, but nobody can tell when the project is done or whether the design meets them.

qs.s: Read the migration plan from a design doc. Which step has no safe rollback?

code.title: Rollout: split users.name into first_name / last_name
code.src:
Step 1: add first_name, last_name columns (nullable). Deploy.
Step 2: app writes to name AND first/last. Backfill old rows.
Step 3: app reads first/last; still writes all three. Deploy.
Step 4: in one deploy, stop writing name and drop the name column.

o: Step 1, because adding columns locks the table
Step 2, because the backfill cannot be stopped
Step 3, because reads change
Step 4: once the column is dropped, rolling back the app to code that reads name fails, and the data is gone
qs.e: Steps 1–3 can each be undone by deploying the previous version, because old and new code both still work. Step 4 combines the switch and the destructive change. The safe pattern (expand, migrate, contract) stops writing first, waits a few days, and drops the column in a separate, late step after a backup.

qs.s: A design doc changes the format of order events that the data team's pipeline and the finance reports consume. The reviewer list is only the author's own team. What is the most important fix?
o: Add the data team and finance-report owners as required reviewers with the same review deadline, and add a “Who is affected” section
Add more diagrams so the data team can understand it later
Ship it and announce the change in the release notes
Make the doc shorter so it is reviewed faster
qs.e: The people who will break are consumers outside the team, so they must review before the change. Release notes inform them after the damage. Diagrams and length do not help if the affected people never see the doc.

qs.s: Read the Alternatives section. What should a reviewer say?

code.title: Design doc: Notifications service, section 7
code.src:
7. Alternatives considered

(a) Keep sending emails directly from each service.
    Rejected: messy.

(b) Build our own SMTP server.
    Rejected: too much work.

Therefore we will build a new notifications service with
Kafka, a template engine and a preferences UI.

o: Nothing; two alternatives are listed, which meets the template
Ask for a cost estimate of option (b)
The alternatives are straw men. Ask for a real competitor, such as a shared library or a managed notification provider, compared on cost, effort and risk, and say what is “messy” in numbers
Ask the author to remove the section, because the decision is already made
qs.e: Alternatives are only useful if they are serious options. Here the strongest cheaper options (a small shared module, or buying) are missing, and “messy” cannot be checked. Filling the template is not the goal; the reader must believe the chosen design beat real competition.

interview.q: When do you write a design doc, and when is a PR description enough?
answer: Write one when the work is hard to reverse, crosses team boundaries, changes stored data or a public API, or takes more than a couple of weeks.
A short PR description is enough for local, reversible changes.
Length should match risk: a 1–3 page mini doc for medium work; longer only for large projects (Google's guidance mentions around 10–20 pages as the upper sweet spot).
The doc is a tool to find mistakes early, not a gate; if it would not change any decision, skip it.
followups: How do you keep design docs from slowing the team down?
What happens to the doc after the project ships?

interview.q: Your design doc review has stalled for three weeks. How do you get to a decision?
answer: Make sure the doc names one approver and a review end date in the header.
Summarise the open disagreements at the top, each with the options and trade-offs.
Hold one short meeting with the approver and the people who disagree, only on those points.
Record the decision and the reasoning in the doc (or an ADR) and move on; reviewers can disagree and commit.
If the disagreement is about unknowns, propose a small spike or prototype to get data.
followups: What if the approver is the person blocking?
How do you handle a reviewer who comments only on small things?

interview.q: What do you look for first when you review someone else's design doc?
answer: Is the problem real and stated with data, and are the goals measurable, with non-goals?
Has the hardest part been found and addressed, or is it hidden in one line?
Rollout and rollback: can each step be undone without data loss? Is there a migration plan for existing data?
Operations: metrics, alerts, on-call impact, cost at expected scale.
Who is affected and whether they are reviewers; security and privacy where data is involved.
followups: Give an example of a design issue you caught in review.
How do you give hard feedback on a senior colleague's doc?

diagrams.title: Design-doc review flow
diagrams.src:
flowchart TD A["Write problem, goals, non-goals"] --> B["Share draft
named approver + deadline"] B --> C["Async comments from owners
of affected systems"] C --> D{"Open disagreements?"} D -- yes --> E["30-min meeting
for those only"] D -- no --> F["Approver decides"] E --> F F --> G["Record outcome
in the doc or an ADR"] G --> H["Build behind a flag"]
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the meeting is optional and narrow. Most review happens in comments, and the flow always ends in a recorded decision by one named approver.

codeCheck.detail: A document skeleton, not code. Review date 2026-10-14 is a Wednesday; nothing else to execute.

videos.t: What Is A Design Doc In Software Engineering? (full example)
videos.why: What a design doc is, with a full example.

one: Reviewing for correctness, design and knowledge-sharing, while keeping reviews fast and kind enough that the team keeps shipping.
an: An editor improving a manuscript, not a judge grading it. The goal is a better book and a better writer.
how: Prioritise: correctness and security → design and data model → tests → readability. Automate style (formatters, linters) so humans never discuss it.
Label severity: blocking vs nit vs question. Explain why, suggest alternatives, and praise good choices specifically.
Speed matters: aim to respond within hours. Small PRs (under ~400 lines) get better reviews; ask for splits.
Review the PR description and tests first; they show intent.
why: Review is the main daily channel for raising code quality and growing juniors. Slow or harsh reviews are a top cause of team frustration.
trade: Gatekeeping every PR yourself does not scale. Grow other reviewers and trust them.

myth.m: A good review finds lots of issues.
myth.r: A good review finds the important issues quickly. Twenty nits bury the one bug that mattered.

q.s: A junior's PR works but uses a pattern you would not choose, with no correctness issue. Best review approach?
o: Block until rewritten your way
Approve, optionally leave a non-blocking suggestion explaining the trade-off
Ignore the PR
Rewrite it yourself
q.e: Block on correctness and real risk. Preferences are teaching moments, not gates.

more: What to look for in order of importance
lab: Review three open-source PRs in a project you use (read only). For each, write down your top comment and whether it is blocking. Then compare with the maintainers' actual comments.

plain:
Code review is reading a teammate's change before it merges, to catch problems and share knowledge. As a lead, you set the tone: focus on what matters, be quick, be kind, and teach.

Order of importance: correctness and security, then design, then tests, then readability. Formatting should be automated, not discussed.
bridge: You have received reviews with 25 comments about naming and missed the one real bug. A good review is the opposite: few comments, the important ones clearly marked.

walk.title: Reviewing a junior's PR well
steps: Read the PR description and the tests first, to understand the intent.
Find one real issue: the endpoint does not check that the order belongs to the user. Mark it blocking and explain the risk.
Notice a pattern you would write differently but that works: leave it as a non-blocking suggestion with the reason.
Point out one thing done well, specifically.
Approve once the blocking issue is fixed. Total time: 20 minutes, response within a few hours.

terms: Smaller PRs get better reviews; aim for a few hundred lines.
Labelling comments by type (issue, suggestion, question, praise).
insights: Watch two numbers: time to first review and PR size. When either grows, quality drops before anyone complains.
A review that finds nothing on a 2,000-line PR is a warning sign, not a good result.
Your own comments set the team's tone: model labels, reasons and specific praise.

prod.summary: In a healthy team, review is fast, small and focused on risk: a first response within one business day (Google's published maximum), PRs small enough to read in one sitting, and comments clearly labelled as blocking or not. Leads watch the system, not only single PRs: time to first review, PR size, and whether review knowledge is spread across the team or stuck with one person.
checklist: Read the PR description and tests first: is the intent clear, and do the tests prove the behaviour, including failure cases?
Check the high-risk areas: authorisation (does this user own this object?), input validation, money and time zones, migrations on large tables, concurrency, and secrets in code or logs.
Check backwards compatibility: API shape, database migrations that old code must survive during deploy, feature-flag default.
Label every comment: blocking issue, suggestion, question, or nit, so the author knows what must change.
Ask for a split when a PR mixes refactor and behaviour change, or is too big to review in about an hour.
Formatting and style are enforced by Prettier/ESLint in CI, never by humans.
Approve when it is better than the current code and safe, not when it matches your personal style.
numbers: Google's engineering practices: “One business day is the maximum time it should take to respond to a code review request.”
Google's small-CL guide: “100 lines is usually a reasonable size for a CL, and 1000 lines is usually too large.”
SmartBear's study of 2,500 reviews at Cisco: review 200–400 lines at a time; defect detection drops after 60–90 minutes of review and at speeds above about 500 lines per hour.
GitHub branch protection can require a number of approving reviews and review from CODEOWNERS before merge.
failures: PRs wait 3 days for review; developers open 4 PRs in parallel and spend their time rebasing.

Review is treated as an interruption, and one lead reviews everything. Set a team norm (first response same or next working day), add a daily review slot, and use CODEOWNERS with several owners per area so the load is shared.
A 2,400-line PR gets “LGTM” in 10 minutes. A week later, an endpoint leaks other customers' orders.
Large PRs get skimmed, so the authorisation bug was missed. Ask for a split (refactor first, then behaviour), and add a review checklist item: “every new query that takes an ID checks ownership.”
A junior engineer stops asking for reviews from one senior and the team quietly routes around them.

Review comments are harsh or unlabelled, so every nit feels like a blocker. Use labels (Conventional Comments), explain the why, and give feedback on tone in private. Leads should model this in their own reviews.
A migration runs ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN region SET NOT NULL on a 50M-row table. Review approved it; during deploy all writes to orders hang for minutes.

SET NOT NULL scans the whole table while holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. (Adding a new column with a constant default is fast since PostgreSQL 11; changing an existing column is not.) Safe pattern: add CHECK (region IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (weaker lock), then SET NOT NULL, which skips the scan on PostgreSQL 12+. Make migrations a review area with its own owner, and set lock_timeout in migrations.

code.title: Review comments with clear labels (Conventional Comments style)
code.src:
issue (blocking): GET /orders/:id loads the order by id only.
  Any logged-in user can read any order by changing the id.
  Please add `where: { id, userId: session.userId }` and a test
  that a second user gets 404.

question (non-blocking): Why retry the webhook 10 times without delay?
  If the provider is down, we send 10 requests in 1 second.
  Would exponential backoff via the existing job queue work here?

suggestion (non-blocking): This reduce is correct but hard to read.
  A plain for...of loop would be clearer. Fine to keep if you prefer.

nitpick (non-blocking): `data2` -> `pendingRefunds`?

praise: The test for the expired-token case is exactly the edge
  case I would have missed. Thank you.
code.note: Only the first comment blocks the merge, and it explains the risk and the fix. Everything else is clearly optional, so the author can ship as soon as the real issue is fixed.

qs.s: Your team's dashboard shows median time to first review = 26 hours and median PR size = 900 changed lines. Which change will most likely improve both quality and speed?
o: Require two approvals instead of one
Ask authors to split work into smaller PRs (for example under ~400 lines) and agree a same-or-next-day first response norm
Ban PRs on Fridays
Let authors merge without review if CI passes
qs.e: Large PRs are slow to review and get skimmed; small PRs are reviewed faster and more carefully. Two approvals doubles the waiting. Skipping review removes the safety net instead of fixing the cause.

qs.s: You review this handler: const user = await db.user.findUnique({ where: { id: req.params.id } }); return res.json(user); in an endpoint any logged-in user can call. What is the most important comment?
o: Rename user to foundUser
Use findFirst instead of findUnique
Blocking: there is no check that the caller may read this user, and the full row (maybe including the password hash) is returned; check access and select only public fields
Add a JSDoc comment
qs.e: This is an access-control bug (anyone can read any user) plus data over-exposure. Both are security issues and must block. The other comments are style or no improvement at all.

qs.s: As a lead you are the required reviewer on every PR in a team of 8. Reviews take 2 hours of your day and PRs wait for you. What is the best long-term fix?
o: Review faster by skipping the tests
Hire a dedicated QA engineer to do reviews
Stop doing reviews and rely on CI
Make several engineers code owners for each area, pair-review with them for a few weeks, and keep yourself as required reviewer only for high-risk areas
qs.e: Spreading review ownership removes the bottleneck and grows judgement in the team. Skipping tests lowers quality; QA does not replace design review; stopping review loses knowledge sharing and risk checks.

qs.s: You review this handler for transferring credits between two users. Which comment must block the merge?

code.title: transfer.ts

o: Nit: rename from to sender
Suggestion: add a JSDoc comment explaining the parameters
Question: why not return the new balance?

Blocking: the check and the two updates are not in one transaction, and the balance is written from a stale read. Two parallel transfers can both pass the check and overspend, and a crash between updates loses money. Use a transaction with an atomic conditional decrement, and validate amount > 0
qs.e: This is a money bug under concurrency: read-then-write with a stale value is a lost update, and two separate updates are not atomic. A negative amount would also move money the wrong way. The other comments are optional style points; marking them the same as this bug would hide it.

qs.s: Which of these review comments should be labelled blocking?

code.title: Comments on PR #1290 (add CSV export)
code.src:
1. The export loads all rows with findMany() and builds the
   CSV in memory. Our biggest customer has 3M orders.
2. I would name this function exportOrdersCsv instead of doExport.
3. Could we use the csv-stringify library instead of join(",")?
   Values with commas or quotes will break the file.
4. Nice test for the empty-export case.

o: Only 2, because naming affects every future reader
1 and 3: the memory problem will crash the server for the biggest customer, and unescaped commas or quotes produce corrupt files
All four, so the author takes the review seriously
None; the author can fix things in a follow-up PR
qs.e: Block on correctness and production risk: an out-of-memory crash and corrupt CSV for real data. Naming is a suggestion and praise is not an action. Marking everything blocking teaches authors that labels mean nothing.

qs.s: A 1,200-line PR arrives. Using SmartBear's Cisco findings (useful review speed up to about 400–500 lines per hour, attention drops after 60–90 minutes), what should you do?
o: Review it in one 20-minute pass, focusing on the tests
Approve; large PRs are normal for features
Ask for a split: at a useful pace it needs about 2.5–3 hours, well past the point where reviewers stop finding defects. Suggest a refactor-only PR, then the behaviour change
Ask two reviewers to each skim half
qs.e: 1,200 ÷ 400–500 lines/hour ≈ 2.4–3 hours, far beyond 60–90 minutes of effective attention, so defects get missed. Splitting by intent makes each part reviewable. Two people skimming halves still miss bugs that sit between the halves.

qs.s: A PR contains this migration for a 50M-row orders table on PostgreSQL 16. What is the correct review comment?

code.title: migrations/0142_region_not_null.sql
code.src:
-- column already exists and is fully backfilled
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN region SET NOT NULL;

o: Blocking: this scans the whole table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so writes stop. Add CHECK (region IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, then SET NOT NULL (no scan on PostgreSQL 12+), with a lock_timeout
Approve: since PostgreSQL 11, NOT NULL changes are metadata-only
Blocking: it will rewrite the whole table and double its disk size
Approve, but run it at night
qs.e: PostgreSQL 11 made adding a new column with a constant default fast; it did not change SET NOT NULL on an existing column, which must check every row while holding the strongest lock. It does not rewrite the table, though. Running at night reduces impact but writes still stop, and many products have no quiet night.

interview.q: What do you look for when you review a PR, and in what order?
answer: Start with the description and tests to understand intent; check that tests cover failure cases.
Then correctness and security: authorisation on every ID from the client, input validation, concurrency, money and time zones, secrets in logs.
Then data and compatibility: migrations on big tables, API changes that old clients or old code must survive during deploy.
Then design and readability. Style is the linter's job.
Label each comment (blocking, suggestion, nit) so the author knows what must change.
followups: How do you review a PR in an area you do not know well?
What is a review comment you regret?

interview.q: Reviews on your team are slow. How would you fix it?
answer: Measure first: time to first review, PR size, and who does the reviews.
Set a norm, for example a first response within one business day (Google's maximum), and a daily review slot.
Make PRs smaller: split refactors from behaviour changes; use stacked PRs or feature flags for big features.
Spread ownership with CODEOWNERS listing several people per area, so one person is not the bottleneck.
Automate style and simple checks in CI so humans review only what needs judgement.
followups: Would you require two approvals? Why or why not?
How would you treat urgent hotfix PRs?

interview.q: How do you give review feedback to someone who takes it badly, or to someone more senior than you?
answer: Comment on the code and its effect, not the person; explain the risk behind each blocking comment.
Ask questions when you are unsure (“what happens if two requests arrive at once?”) instead of stating opinions as facts.
Separate must-fix from preference with labels; approve when the code is safe even if you would write it differently.
Move long disagreements to a short call, then write the outcome in the PR.
Point out what is done well, specifically.
followups: What if the author refuses a blocking comment?
How do you notice that your reviews discourage people?

diagrams.title: How to label a review comment
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the order of questions is the order of importance (correctness and security, then design and tests, then style). Only the first branch is always blocking.

videos.why: How a staff engineer actually reviews code.

one: Giving useful forecasts under uncertainty, slicing work into small deliverable pieces, and surfacing risk early.
an: A weather forecast: "70% chance of rain" is useful and honest. "It will rain at 3:12pm" is false precision.
how: Break work down until pieces are a day or two; unknowns become explicit spikes (time-boxed investigations).
Give ranges with confidence ("2–4 weeks, 80% confident; the risk is the payment provider's sandbox").
Vertical slices: deliver thin end-to-end features (UI + API + DB for one case) rather than horizontal layers. Value and feedback arrive early.
Track and re-forecast; raise slippage as soon as you see it, with options (cut scope, add time, accept risk).
why: Trust between engineering and the business is built on predictable delivery and early bad news, not on optimistic dates.
trade: Estimates become commitments in people's heads. Separate them explicitly, and attach assumptions.

myth.r: Good engineers estimate honestly, decompose well, and communicate changes early. Accuracy comes from smaller pieces, not talent.

q.s: Two weeks into a 6-week project you discover the integration will take twice as long. Best move?
o: Work weekends and hope
Tell stakeholders now with options: cut scope, move the date, or add help
Wait until week 5
Quietly drop tests
q.e: Early bad news with options is a leadership skill; late bad news destroys trust.

lab: Take a feature you are about to build. Split it into vertical slices of at most 2 days each. Estimate each as a range. After shipping, compare actual vs estimate and note where the gap came from.

plain: Estimating means giving a useful forecast while things are uncertain. Good estimates are ranges with a confidence (“2–4 weeks, fairly confident; the risk is the bank API”), built from small pieces of work. When reality changes, you say so early, with options.
bridge: Your sprint tickets are estimates. The senior skill is breaking big unclear work into small clear pieces and telling stakeholders about slippage the day you see it, not the day before the deadline.

walk.title: Planning a payments integration
steps: Unknown: how the provider's sandbox and webhooks behave. Do a 2-day spike first to find out.
Split into vertical slices: (1) create a payment and redirect, (2) handle success webhook, (3) failures and retries, (4) refunds, (5) monthly reconciliation.
Estimate each as a range; total 3–5 weeks.
Week 2: the provider's webhooks are unreliable. Tell the product manager immediately: options are cut refunds from v1, add one week, or add a daily reconciliation job.
They choose to cut refunds from v1. Delivery is on time, and trust goes up.

terms: A short time-boxed investigation of an unknown.
A thin piece of a feature working end to end.
What is included in a delivery.
insights: Forecast from real throughput (slices finished per week), not by re-guessing the remaining work.
Write the assumptions next to the estimate; when one breaks, re-estimate that day.
Once a number leaves the room it becomes a date. Give it in writing, as a range, with what would change it.

prod.summary: In real teams, estimates are forecasts that leadership turns into plans, contracts and marketing dates, so how you give them matters as much as the number. Seniors break work into small vertical slices, run time-boxed spikes on the unknowns first, give ranges with named risks, and re-forecast every week with real progress data. Bad news is shared the day it is known, together with options.
checklist: The biggest unknown (third-party API, data migration, performance) has a spike scheduled first, not last.
Work is split into vertical slices of 1–3 days, each deployable (behind a flag if needed) and demoable.
The estimate is a range with a confidence level and the assumptions written next to it.
The estimate includes the work people forget: tests, migrations, observability, review time, deploy and rollout, documentation, support handover.
Progress is tracked by slices done, not by percentage “90% done” claims.
A re-forecast happens weekly; a slip of more than ~20% triggers a message to stakeholders with options (cut scope, move date, add help, accept risk).
Fixed dates get flexible scope: the team agrees in advance which slices are “must” and which can be cut.
numbers: Steve McConnell's cone of uncertainty: at the initial concept stage, estimates can be off by a factor of 4 in either direction (0.25x to 4x); the range narrows only as requirements and design become concrete.
Basecamp's Shape Up fixes time and varies scope: a big batch is 6 weeks, followed by a 2-week cool-down.
Brooks's law (The Mythical Man-Month, 1975): adding people to a late software project makes it later, because new people need ramp-up and add communication paths.
failures: Every ticket is “90% done” for three weeks; the demo is postponed twice.

Work was split by layer (all backend, then all frontend), so nothing was finished end to end. Re-slice into vertical slices and measure only shipped slices. The remaining 10% is usually integration that was never estimated.
The sales team promised a customer a date that was the engineer's best-case guess from a hallway chat.

A single number was given without a range or assumptions, and it became a commitment. Always answer with a range and confidence in writing (“4–7 weeks, 70% confident, assuming the bank sandbox works”), and say what would change it.
Week 5 of 6: the team discovers the payment provider's webhooks are not delivered in order. The launch slips three weeks.
The riskiest integration was planned last. Do a 2–3 day spike on unknown external systems in week 1, and schedule the risky slice early so surprises arrive while there is still time to act.
The project is late, so two engineers from another team join for the last month. Velocity drops further.
Brooks's law: onboarding and coordination cost more than the new help in the short term. Cut scope instead, or add people early, onto work that is truly separate.

code.title: A forecast stakeholders can actually use
code.src:
Project: Card payments via new provider
Forecast (2026-10-02): ships 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-20, ~75% confident

Slices (done / remaining):
  [done] 1. Spike: sandbox, auth, webhook format (2 days)
  [done] 2. Create payment + redirect, behind flag
  [ 3d ] 3. Success webhook + idempotent order update
  [ 4d ] 4. Failure + retry handling
  [ 3d ] 5. Refunds                       <- can be cut from v1
  [ 2d ] 6. Daily reconciliation report
  [ 3d ] 7. Rollout: 5% -> 50% -> 100%, alerts, runbook

Assumptions:
  - Provider production keys arrive by 2026-10-20.
  - One backend engineer is on-call 1 week in 4.

Risks:
  - Webhook delivery order is not guaranteed (found in spike).
    Mitigation: idempotent handler + reconciliation (slice 6).

If we must hit 2026-11-06: ship without refunds (slice 5);
support handles refunds manually in the provider dashboard.
code.note: The last two lines turn a date argument into a choice: the business picks between scope and time, and the engineering team does not silently absorb the risk.

qs.s: A product manager asks “how long for SSO login?” You have never integrated their identity provider. What is the best first answer?
o: “I need a 2-day spike to test the provider; after that I can give a range with confidence”, and give a rough range now, clearly labelled as low confidence
“2 weeks” so planning can start
“It is impossible to estimate”
“Same as the last auth feature, about 3 weeks”
qs.e: The biggest unknown is the external system, so a short time-boxed spike reduces uncertainty fast. A rough labelled range still helps planning. A single number becomes a promise; refusing gives the business nothing; copying an old estimate ignores the new risk.

qs.s: You have 12 slices left. Over the last 3 weeks the team finished 3, 4 and 2 slices. Roughly when will the project finish, as a range?
o: In 1 week
In about 3–6 weeks (12 ÷ 4 = 3 at the best rate, 12 ÷ 2 = 6 at the worst)
Exactly 4 weeks
In 12 weeks
qs.e: Using real throughput gives a range: the best week (4) means 3 weeks, the worst week (2) means 6 weeks; the average (3/week) gives 4. Giving only 4 hides the variance; the other answers ignore the data.

qs.s: A fixed launch date is set by a conference. At the halfway point you are 30% behind. Which plan is most realistic?
o: Add three engineers from another team for the final weeks
Ask everyone to work weekends until launch
Agree with the product owner which “must” slices ship at the conference and move the rest to a follow-up release
Skip testing and code review to save time
qs.e: When the date cannot move, scope must. Late extra people usually slow things down first (Brooks's law); weekends burn people and raise bugs; skipping tests moves the cost to production incidents.

qs.s: Read this project status. What is the best conclusion?

code.title: Weekly status, week 5 of 6
code.src:
Backend API ........ 90% done
Database schema .... 100% done
Frontend screens ... 85% done
Integration ........ not started
QA ................. not started

Overall: 85% complete, on track

o: The project is not on track: nothing works end to end, integration and QA have not started, and percentages per layer hide the hardest remaining work
The project is on track, since the average is above 80%
The project needs one more frontend developer for a week
The status is fine but should use story points instead of percentages
qs.e: Work split by layer reaches “90%” quickly while the risky part (integration) waits. Track finished vertical slices that work end to end. Story points have the same problem if no slice is finished. Adding a person in the last week usually slows things down first.

qs.s: You estimate a task with three points: optimistic 4 weeks, most likely 6 weeks, pessimistic 14 weeks. Using the PERT formula (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6, what is the expected duration, and what does it show?
o: 6 weeks; the most likely value is the right answer
8 weeks, the average of the three values
7 weeks; the long pessimistic tail pulls the expected value above the most likely one
4 weeks, because PERT uses the optimistic value
qs.e: (4 + 4×6 + 14) ÷ 6 = 42 ÷ 6 = 7 weeks. Real tasks can overrun much more than they can underrun, so the expected value is above the most likely one. Giving “6 weeks” as a date sets a target you will miss more often than not. A simple average (8) gives the tail too much weight.

qs.s: An engineer estimates a feature at “5 days” by counting only coding time. Which list is most often missing from such estimates?
o: Time to choose variable names
Tests, code review waiting time, database migration, observability, rollout steps, and documentation or support handover
Time for the product manager to write the ticket
Time for CI to run once
qs.e: Coding is often less than half of the delivery work. Review waiting, migrations and rollout regularly double a coding-only estimate. A checklist of these items next to every estimate is a cheap fix.

qs.s: You get this message. You think 6 Nov has about a 50% chance. What is the best reply?

code.title: Slack, #payments-launch
code.src:
Dilnoza (Product), 10:14
Marketing wants to announce the new payment flow on 6 Nov.
Can you commit to 6 Nov? Need a yes/no today.

o: “Yes”, because a no would block marketing
“No”, because a missed date is worse than a late one
“I can't commit to any date until we are finished”

“6 Nov is about 50/50 with full scope; 20 Nov is ~80%. If 6 Nov is fixed, we can hit it by shipping without refunds (support does them manually). Which do you prefer? I'll confirm after the provider test on Tuesday.”
qs.e: A yes/no hides the real uncertainty and makes the business carry hidden risk. A range with confidence, a scope option for the fixed date, and when you will know more turns it into a business choice. Refusing any date gives marketing nothing to plan with.

interview.q: How do you estimate a project with a lot of unknowns?
answer: Find the biggest unknowns first (third-party APIs, data migration, performance) and run short time-boxed spikes on them.
Break the rest into vertical slices of 1–3 days; estimate slices, not the whole.
Give a range with a confidence level and write the assumptions next to it.
Expect early estimates to be very wide: McConnell's cone of uncertainty shows estimates at the initial-concept stage can be off by about 4x in either direction, and that is a best case.
Re-forecast from real throughput (slices finished per week) once work starts.
followups: How do you answer when someone wants one number?
Do you use story points? Why or why not?

interview.q: Your project is going to be late. What do you do?
answer: Tell stakeholders the day you know, not the day before the deadline.
Bring options with their costs: cut or defer scope, move the date, add help (with Brooks's law in mind), accept a risk.
Make a recommendation, and let the owner of the priority decide; write the decision down.
Find the cause (unplanned work, a wrong assumption, interrupts) and fix how you estimate next time.
followups: When does adding people actually help?
How do you protect the team from working weekends?

interview.q: How do you plan delivery for a date that cannot move, like a conference launch?
answer: Fix time, vary scope: agree up front which slices are “must” and which can be cut.
Build the riskiest and most important slices first, so cuts fall on the least valuable work.
Keep everything deployable behind feature flags so you can release what is ready.
Set check-points (for example every week) where you decide on cuts using real progress.
Keep tests and review; skipping them moves the cost into launch-day incidents.
followups: What if the product manager says everything is a must?
How does Shape Up handle this?

one: Research-backed measures of software delivery performance from Google's DORA program. The classic four keys are deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail rate and recovery time; since 2024 DORA uses five, adding deployment rework rate.
an: A car's speed and its brakes measured together. Going fast only counts if you can also stop safely.
how: Throughput (dora.dev grouping): change lead time (commit to running in production), deployment frequency, and failed deployment recovery time (how long it takes to recover from a deployment that needs immediate intervention; formerly “time to restore service”/MTTR).

Instability: change fail rate (share of deployments that need immediate intervention, such as a rollback or hotfix) and deployment rework rate (share of deployments that are unplanned and happen because of a production incident).

DORA's research has repeatedly found that speed and stability are not a trade-off: top performers do well on all metrics, low performers do poorly on all. Small batches, automated testing and deployment, and good monitoring drive both.
Measure per application or service. Comparing a mobile app with a mainframe, or ranking teams, is misleading and invites gaming.
why: It gives leads a shared, evidence-based language for improving the delivery system (and for arguing for CI/CD investment) instead of judging individuals.
trade: Metrics used to rank people get gamed. Use them for the team's own improvement, alongside how developers actually feel (surveys).

myth.m: Moving faster always means more incidents.
myth.r: DORA's data shows the opposite pattern: teams that deploy small changes often also tend to have lower change fail rates and recover faster. But speed without safety nets does hurt: the 2024 and 2025 reports found AI adoption linked to lower delivery stability, likely because it makes larger changes easier.

q.s: Your team deploys monthly, and 30% of deploys cause incidents. What does DORA research suggest?
o: Deploy even less often
Ship smaller batches more often, with automation and fast rollback
Add a change approval board
Freeze code
q.e: Large infrequent batches are riskier. Shrinking batch size improves both stability and speed.

more: Measuring each metric from git and deploy logs
The 2024 change: five metrics and rework rate
2025: seven team archetypes instead of low/medium/high/elite
Capabilities that drive the metrics (CI, trunk-based development, loosely coupled architecture)
lab: Calculate deployment frequency, lead time and change fail rate for one project from git log and deploy history for the last month.
docs: DORA: Software delivery performance metrics guide

plain:
DORA metrics measure how well a team delivers software, based on more than ten years of research. Since 2024 there are five. Throughput (how fast change flows): how often you deploy, how long a change takes from commit to production, and how fast you recover when a deploy breaks something. Instability (how often change goes wrong): how often a deploy needs an urgent fix, and how often you ship unplanned fixes for incidents.

The key finding: the best teams are good at both speed and stability at the same time.
bridge: If your team deploys once a month in a stressful “release day”, these metrics explain why that feels risky: big batches fail more and take longer to fix.

walk.title: Measuring your own team
steps: Deployment frequency: count production deploys of one service last month. Say 5: 4 planned releases and 1 urgent hotfix.
Change lead time: median time from commit to production. Say 6 days (changes wait for the weekly release).
Change fail rate: 1 of the 5 deploys broke checkout and needed immediate intervention, so 1 ÷ 5 = 20%.
Failed deployment recovery time: the hotfix restored checkout after 5 hours. Deployment rework rate: the hotfix was an unplanned deploy caused by that incident, so 1 ÷ 5 = 20%.
Improvement plan: automate deploys and ship each merge; add a canary and one-click rollback. Next quarter's target: 40 deploys, 1-day lead time, lower fail rate, 30-minute recovery.

terms: How often you release to production.
Time from commit to running in production.
Share of deployments that need immediate intervention (rollback, hotfix).
How long it takes to recover from a failed deployment (formerly “time to restore”, MTTR).
Share of deployments that are unplanned fixes for a production incident.
insights: Read the five together: frequency rising while fail rate also rises means batches got riskier, not that delivery improved.
Split lead time into working and waiting stages; in most teams the waits (review, release train) are longer than the coding.
One-click rollback is usually the cheapest way to cut recovery time; fixing forward under pressure is slow.

prod.summary: In production, DORA metrics come from data you already have: the CI/CD system (deploy events), git (commit times) and the incident tracker (which deploy caused what). Leads use them per service, over weeks, to find the bottleneck in the delivery pipeline: waiting for a weekly release, slow review, flaky tests, or risky big-batch deploys. They are a diagnosis tool for the team, not a scoreboard for people.
checklist: Deploy events are recorded automatically by the pipeline (service, commit SHA, time, result), not by hand.
“Failure” has one written definition: a deploy that needed a rollback, hotfix or fix-forward to restore service.
Incidents are linked to the deploy that caused them, so change fail rate and recovery time can be calculated.
Metrics are viewed per service and as trends (4-week rolling), not as one number for the whole company.
Lead time is split into stages (coding, waiting for review, review, waiting for deploy) to find where time is lost.
Nobody's performance review uses these numbers; they are paired with a developer-experience survey.
When AI coding tools are rolled out, PR size and change fail rate are watched for regressions.
numbers: dora.dev now lists five metrics: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate, deployment rework rate.
2024 DORA report: a 25% increase in AI adoption was associated with an estimated 1.5% decrease in delivery throughput and a 7.2% decrease in delivery stability.

2025 DORA report (nearly 5,000 respondents): 90% use AI at work; AI adoption now relates positively to throughput but still negatively to stability. The report replaced the low/medium/high/elite tiers with seven team archetypes.
failures: Deployment frequency doubled in one quarter after it became a team OKR, but customers see no faster delivery.

The metric was gamed: empty or config-only deploys, or one feature split into many trivial deploys. Look at lead time and change fail rate together with frequency, and remove the metric from targets tied to rewards.
Change fail rate shows 0% for six months, yet the on-call channel is full of incidents.
Incidents are not linked to deploys, so failures are never counted. Add a required “caused by deploy” field to the incident template (or “not deploy-related”) and backfill the last quarter.
Lead time is 9 days. The team assumes coding is slow and starts a refactor.

Nobody split lead time by stage. A breakdown often shows PRs waiting 3–4 days for review and merged code waiting for a weekly release train. Fix the waits (review norms, deploy on merge) before touching code.
After an AI assistant rollout, PRs are 3x larger and the change fail rate rises from 8% to 18%.
Bigger batches carry more risk, which matches DORA's 2024–2025 findings. Keep PR size limits, require tests for generated code, and use canary releases with automatic rollback.

code.title: Four DORA metrics for one service from your own tables (PostgreSQL)
code.src:
-- deployments(id, service, deployed_at, needed_intervention bool, is_unplanned_fix bool)
-- deploy_commits(deploy_id, sha);  commits(sha, committed_at)
-- incidents(id, caused_by_deploy_id, opened_at, resolved_at)
WITH d AS (
  SELECT * FROM deployments
  WHERE service = 'checkout'
    AND deployed_at >= now() - interval '28 days'
)
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM d) / 4.0 AS deploys_per_week,
  (SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY d.deployed_at - c.committed_at)
     FROM d
     JOIN deploy_commits dc ON dc.deploy_id = d.id
     JOIN commits c ON c.sha = dc.sha) AS median_change_lead_time,
  (SELECT round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE needed_intervention)
                / nullif(count(*), 0), 1) FROM d) AS change_fail_pct,
  (SELECT round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_unplanned_fix)
                / nullif(count(*), 0), 1) FROM d) AS rework_pct,
  (SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY i.resolved_at - i.opened_at)
     FROM incidents i JOIN d ON d.id = i.caused_by_deploy_id) AS median_recovery_time;
code.note: Lead time is measured per commit, not per deploy, so one big deploy with 40 old commits shows up as a long lead time. nullif avoids division by zero in a month with no deploys.

qs.s: Team A deploys 30 times a week with a 15% change fail rate. Team B deploys once a month with a 15% change fail rate. Both have the same number of customers. Which statement is most accurate?
o: They are equally good, since the change fail rate is the same
Team A has far more failed deploys, but each one is a small change that is usually quicker to find and roll back; Team B's rare failures each contain a month of changes
Team B is better because it has fewer failures
Change fail rate cannot be compared at different frequencies
qs.e: Same percentage, very different shape. Small batches make failures easier to diagnose and recover from, which is why DORA pairs fail rate with recovery time. Counting failures alone ignores how big and how long each one is.

qs.s: A director wants a dashboard ranking the 12 engineers by deployment frequency and change fail rate for performance reviews. What is the best response?
o: Agree, but use 3-month averages
Agree, but only show the top 3
Use only change fail rate, since it measures quality

Explain that DORA metrics describe a team's delivery system, not individuals; ranking people will get them gamed (tiny deploys, hidden incidents). Offer team-level trends plus a developer survey instead
qs.e: DORA metrics measure the system at application or service level. Tying them to individual reviews changes behaviour: people split deploys or stop linking incidents. Averaging or showing fewer people does not fix that.

qs.s: Your lead time breakdown: coding 1 day, waiting for first review 3 days, review 0.5 days, waiting for the Thursday release 2.5 days. What is the best first improvement?
o: Buy faster CI machines
Ask engineers to code faster
Set a next-working-day review norm and deploy automatically on merge, removing about 5 of the 7 days
Add a change approval board to reduce failures
qs.e: Most of the lead time (5.5 of 7 days) is waiting, not work. Fixing the queues gives the biggest gain. Faster CI or coding attacks a small part; an approval board adds more waiting and DORA research has not found it to improve stability.

qs.s: Read these numbers for one service. What are the change fail rate and the deployment rework rate?

code.title: checkout-service, last 4 weeks
code.src:
Production deployments ............................. 40
Deployments that needed a rollback or hotfix ......... 6
Deployments that were unplanned fixes for a
  production incident ................................ 5

o: 6% and 5%
qs.e: Change fail rate = 6 ÷ 40 = 15% (deploys that needed immediate intervention). Rework rate = 5 ÷ 40 = 12.5% (unplanned deploys caused by an incident). The hotfix deploys are deploys too, so they stay in the denominator. Swapping the two definitions gives “12.5% and 15%”.

qs.s: A team computes change lead time with this query. What is wrong with it?

code.title: lead_time.sql
code.src:
SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (
         ORDER BY d.deployed_at - pr.merged_at) AS median_lead_time
FROM deployments d
JOIN pull_requests pr ON pr.merge_sha = d.sha
WHERE d.deployed_at > now() - interval '28 days';

o: percentile_cont should be avg
It must also include the time the ticket waited in the backlog
Nothing; merged to deployed is the DORA definition
It starts at merge, so it hides coding and review waiting time; DORA's change lead time starts when the change is committed. It also counts only the merge commit of each PR
qs.e: DORA defines change lead time from commit to running in production. Starting at merge misses the stage where teams usually lose days: waiting for review. Backlog time is not part of the metric (that is a product lead time). A median is the better choice than an average for skewed times.

qs.s: Your cloud provider's database had a 2-hour regional outage. No deployment was involved. How does it affect failed deployment recovery time?
o: It does not count: that metric measures recovery from a failed deployment. Track it as an incident and in your SLO, not in this DORA metric
It counts as 2 hours of recovery time
It counts, and it also raises the change fail rate
It counts only if the team was on call
qs.e: DORA renamed “time to restore service” to “failed deployment recovery time” so that it measures the delivery process. Outages not caused by your changes belong in reliability measures (SLOs, incident reviews). Mixing them in punishes the team for things deployments did not cause.

qs.s: After an AI coding assistant rollout, your dashboard shows this. What is the best next step?

code.title: Team dashboard, quarter over quarter
code.src:
Q2      Q3
Deploys per week         12      15
Median PR size (lines)   140     460
Change fail rate         7%      16%
Median recovery time     40m     2h10m

o: Ban the AI assistant
Bring PR size back down (limits, splitting), require tests on generated code, and add canary releases with automatic rollback; keep watching fail rate and recovery time
Celebrate: deploys per week went up
Lower the deploy frequency to reduce failures
qs.e: Bigger batches carry more risk and are harder to debug, which matches the 2024–2025 DORA findings on AI and stability. Fix batch size and safety nets, not the tool. Deploying less often makes batches even bigger. Looking only at frequency ignores the stability metrics.

interview.q: What are the DORA metrics, and how would you introduce them in a team?
answer: Five metrics on dora.dev: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time (throughput); change fail rate and deployment rework rate (instability).
Collect them automatically from the pipeline, git and the incident tracker, per service.
Agree definitions first: what counts as a deployment and as a failure.
Use them to find the bottleneck (often review waiting or a release train), then fix one thing and watch the trend.
Never use them to rank people or teams, or as targets tied to rewards (Goodhart's law).
followups: Why did DORA replace MTTR with failed deployment recovery time?
How do you measure lead time for a mobile app that ships through an app store?

interview.q: A director wants to raise deployment frequency to “daily for every team by year end”. How do you respond?
answer: Agree with the direction (smaller batches help both speed and stability), but warn that a frequency target alone gets gamed.
Propose improving the capabilities that drive it: CI, automated tests, trunk-based development, deploy on merge, feature flags.
Track frequency together with change fail rate and recovery time, per service.
Accept that context matters: a regulated or mobile service may have different limits.
followups: How would you spot gaming?
What would you do first in a team that deploys monthly?

interview.q: Your lead time is 9 days. How do you find out why?
answer: Split it into stages: coding, waiting for review, review, waiting for merge, waiting for deploy, deploy.
Use timestamps from git, the PR tool and the pipeline; look at medians and the slow tail.
Usually waiting dominates: PRs idle for days, or merged code waiting for a weekly release.
Fix the biggest wait first (review norms, smaller PRs, deploy on merge), then measure again.
followups: What if the slow stage is CI itself?
How do large PRs affect this number?

diagrams.title: Where each DORA metric is measured
diagrams.src:
flowchart TD A["Commit
(lead time starts)"] --> B["Review and merge"] B --> C["Deploy to production
(lead time ends, +1 deploy)"] C --> D{"Needs immediate
intervention?"} D -- no --> E["Change done"] D -- yes --> F["Counts as failed change
(recovery clock starts)"] F --> G["Rollback or hotfix

diagrams.caption: What to notice: all five metrics come from events on this one path, which your CI/CD system, git and incident tracker already record. A cloud outage with no deploy never enters this path, so it does not count.
