one: Deciding whether to build a capability in-house, buy a SaaS, or adopt open source, based on total cost and strategic value.
an: Do you grow your own wheat for the restaurant's bread? Only if the bread is what makes you famous.
how: Build what differentiates your product. Buy commodity (auth, email, payments, monitoring, search) unless constraints forbid it.

Total cost of ownership: building includes maintenance, on-call, security patches and the opportunity cost of what else the team could build. Buying includes fees at scale, lock-in, data residency and vendor risk.
Reduce lock-in with your own interface around the vendor (adapter pattern) and a data export path.
why: A lead's choices here decide where a team's limited engineering time goes for years.
trade: Vendor prices and terms can change; local regulations or unavailable services (e.g. payment providers in a given country) may force building.

myth.m: Building is cheaper because there is no subscription.
myth.r: Engineer-months and ongoing maintenance usually cost far more than the subscription for non-core features.

q.s: A 4-person team plans to build its own authentication system with MFA and social login. Default advice?
o: Build it, auth is easy
Use an established auth provider or library unless a hard constraint forbids it
Skip auth
Store passwords plainly to save time
q.e: Auth is security-critical commodity work. Build what differentiates the product.

more: Security and compliance reviews of vendors
lab: For one capability (auth, email, search, payments), compare building vs two vendors: monthly cost at your scale, engineer-weeks to build, ongoing maintenance, lock-in. Write the recommendation as an ADR.
docs: Martin Fowler: Utility vs strategic dichotomy

plain:
For every capability (login, email, payments, search, analytics), you choose: build it yourself, pay for a service, or use open source. The rule of thumb: build what makes your product special; buy what is common to every product.

Count the full cost: building includes years of maintenance, bugs, security patches and on-call, not just the first version.
bridge: You probably already chose Supabase Auth or Clerk instead of writing your own login, and Netlify instead of running your own servers. That was build vs buy.

walk.title: Should a 4-person team build its own auth?
steps: Requirements: email + password, Google login, MFA, password reset, sessions on web and mobile.
Build estimate: 4–6 weeks to build, plus ongoing security work forever, plus the risk of a security mistake.
Buy: an auth provider at $0–100/month at current scale; a few days to a week to integrate (web and mobile).
Lock-in risk: moderate; mitigated by keeping your own users table and wrapping the provider in an adapter.
Decision: buy. Those 6 weeks go into the features customers pay for.

terms: Making a capability in-house vs using a vendor.
Total cost of ownership over time.
What makes your product better than competitors.
insights: Re-run the decision when its trigger hits (price, scale, a missing feature). Build vs buy is not decided once forever.
“Free” open source still costs servers, upgrades, backups and on-call; count it like a build.
Buying moves work, it does not remove it: integration, vendor reviews, outages and renewals still need an owner.

prod.summary: In real companies build vs buy is a recurring decision with money, security and people attached: a vendor needs a security review, a contract and an exit plan; a build needs headcount, on-call and years of maintenance. Seniors compare total cost over 2–3 years, check the vendor's limits and regional availability against your real requirements, and keep the vendor behind your own interface so you can leave.
checklist: Is this capability a differentiator customers pay for, or commodity work every product needs?
TCO over 2–3 years on both sides: engineer-months to build and maintain (including on-call and security fixes) vs subscription at projected scale (not today's free tier).
Vendor fit: rate limits, SLA, data residency, supported countries and payment methods, compliance (SOC 2 report, GDPR DPA, local data laws).
Exit plan: can you export all data (including password hashes, for auth) in a usable format? How long would migration take?
Your code talks to the vendor through your own interface (adapter), and vendor IDs are stored next to your own IDs.
A failure plan: what happens to your product when the vendor is down for an hour?
The decision and its review trigger (price, scale, a missing feature) are written as an ADR.
numbers: Maintenance after launch commonly takes a meaningful share of the original build effort every year (security patches, upgrades, bug fixes, on-call); estimate it explicitly instead of assuming zero.
Martin Fowler's “utility vs strategic” split: utility functions should be bought or outsourced; only strategic ones deserve in-house investment.
failures: Eighteen months after building an in-house feature-flag system, two engineers spend a third of their time on it, and it still has no audit log or percentage rollout.

The build estimate only counted version one, not the feature parity users expect later. Re-run the TCO with real maintenance hours; migrate to a vendor or a mature open-source tool (e.g. an OpenFeature-compatible one) behind the existing interface.
The email vendor raises prices 4x after an acquisition and the migration takes a quarter, because vendor SDK calls are in 60 files.
No adapter layer. Wrap each vendor in one internal module (sendEmail()), store templates in your repo, and keep a tested second provider for critical flows.
A SaaS chosen in a demo cannot accept local cards in your country, discovered two weeks before launch.
Requirements were not checked against the vendor's real limits. Do a short spike with production-like data and the actual countries, currencies and payment methods before signing.
The vendor's status page shows an outage and your whole sign-up flow is down for 2 hours.
No degradation plan for a hard dependency. Add timeouts, a clear error page, queued retries where possible, and track the vendor's real uptime against its SLA.

code.title: A 3-year TCO comparison you can put in an ADR
code.src:
Capability: authentication (email+password, Google, MFA, sessions)
Scale: 20k MAU today, ~100k MAU in 3 years

BUILD                                       3-year cost
  Initial build: 2 engineers x 6 weeks        ~3 eng-months
  Maintenance per year: security fixes,
    MFA edge cases, upgrades, on-call         M eng-months/yr
    (take M from your history with similar
     systems; never assume 0)
  Security review / pen test of auth code     external quote
  Risk: a credential or session bug           hard to price, high

BUY (auth provider)
  Integration: 1 engineer x 1 week            ~0.25 eng-months
  Fees: from vendor price page at
    20k -> 100k MAU (not the free tier)       $X / year
  Exit: export users incl. password hashes?   yes/no
  Data residency: region options?             yes/no

Decision rule: buy unless 3-year fees + 0.25 eng-months
(integration) > (3 + 3 x M) eng-months of build, or a hard constraint
(residency, country) rules vendors out.
code.note: Fill the vendor fees from the real price page at projected scale, and the maintenance figure from your own team's history. The structure (both sides over 3 years, maintenance included, exit questions) is the point.

qs.s: A 6-person startup sells route-optimisation software for delivery fleets. Which should they most likely build in-house?
o: Transactional email delivery
The routing algorithm and the dispatcher UI around it
Login with MFA
Error monitoring
qs.e: Route optimisation is the product customers pay for, so it deserves engineering time. Email, auth and monitoring are commodity utilities that mature vendors do better and cheaper.

qs.s: You compare an analytics vendor at $400/month with building your own. Engineers estimate 2 weeks to build. What is the most common mistake in this comparison?
o: Forgetting the vendor's onboarding call
Counting the vendor price at current scale only
Assuming the build costs only 2 weeks, ignoring ongoing maintenance, new feature requests and on-call for years
Not asking the vendor for a discount
qs.e: Builds are judged on version one, then live for years. Maintenance, feature parity and on-call usually dwarf the initial estimate. Vendor scale pricing is also worth checking, but the hidden cost of the build is the bigger, more common mistake.

qs.s: You buy an SMS provider for OTP codes. Which design choice gives you the best exit path if prices change or delivery quality drops?
o: Call the vendor SDK directly wherever an SMS is sent
Use the vendor's hosted login page
Store message templates only in the vendor dashboard
Put all SMS sending behind one internal sendSms() interface, keep templates in your repo, and log delivery results in your own database
qs.e: An internal interface keeps the vendor in one place, and owning templates and delivery data means switching is a contained change. The other options spread the vendor through the code or keep your data in their system.

qs.s: Use this comparison (one engineer-month costs $12k). Over 3 years, which option is cheaper, by about how much, before counting risk?

code.title: Feature flags: build vs buy
code.src:
BUILD
  Initial build ........ 3 eng-months
  Maintenance .......... 1.5 eng-months per year

BUY
  Vendor plan .......... $1,500 per month (at projected seats)
  Integration .......... 0.25 eng-months

o: Build, by about $18k, because there is no subscription
Buy, by about $33k: build = (3 + 1.5×3) × $12k = $90k; buy = $54k + $3k = $57k
They cost the same over 3 years
Buy, by about $90k
qs.e: Build: 7.5 eng-months × $12k = $90k. Buy: 36 × $1,500 = $54k plus 0.25 × $12k = $3k, so $57k. The difference is about $33k. Forgetting maintenance makes building look like $36k, which is why “no subscription” is a tempting but wrong argument.

qs.s: An analytics vendor costs $300/month today at 50k monthly events. Your plan expects 2M events per month within 18 months. What should you check before signing?
o: The price at the projected volume, any per-event overage, and contract terms on price increases; a cheap start can become the largest line in the budget
Only today's price, because you can renegotiate later
Whether the vendor's dashboard has dark mode
Whether the vendor is open source
qs.e: Usage-based pricing grows with you, often faster than revenue. Comparing at today's scale is a common mistake. Renegotiating later is weak once your data and code depend on the vendor.

qs.s: You review this “vendor adapter”. What is the main problem?

code.title: email/index.ts

o: It should use a class instead of a function
It does not set a timeout
It is missing a retry loop

It is not a real adapter: callers pass the vendor's message type and receive the vendor's response type, so switching providers still means changing every caller. Define your own input and result types and map inside the module
qs.e: The point of the wrapper is one place to change. Here vendor types leak into every caller, so the lock-in stays. Timeouts and retries matter too, but they do not fix the exit cost. Class vs function is style.

qs.s: Your team wants to self-host an open-source error tracker instead of paying for the SaaS version, because “it's free”. What cost is most often missed?
o: The licence fee
The cost of reading the docs
Running it: servers and storage, upgrades, backups, security patches, and being on call when it breaks, often exactly during your own incidents
Nothing; open source is free
qs.e: Open source removes the licence fee, not the operations work. An error tracker that is down during your outage is worse than none. Self-hosting can still be right (data residency, very large volume), but the comparison must include operations time.

interview.q: How do you decide whether to build or buy something?
answer: First ask whether it differentiates the product. Build what customers choose you for; buy commodity (auth, email, payments, monitoring).
Compare total cost over 2–3 years: build + maintenance + on-call vs fees at projected scale + integration.
Check hard constraints: data residency, countries and payment methods supported, compliance, SLA.
Plan the exit: data export, an internal interface around the vendor.
Write it as an ADR with a revisit trigger (price, scale, missing feature).
followups: Tell me about a build vs buy decision that turned out wrong.
When would you build auth yourself?

interview.q: How do you reduce vendor lock-in?
answer: Put the vendor behind your own module with your own types, so only one place changes.
Keep your own copy of important data (users, templates, delivery logs); store vendor IDs next to your IDs.
Check export options before signing (for auth: can you export password hashes?).
For critical paths, keep a tested second provider or a manual fallback.
Accept some lock-in where the benefit is large; the goal is a known exit cost, not zero lock-in.
followups: Is an adapter always worth it?
How would you migrate between auth providers without logging everyone out?

interview.q: A vendor you depend on goes down for two hours. What should have been in place?
answer: Timeouts and circuit breakers so your service fails fast instead of piling up requests.
Graceful degradation: a clear error message, queued work retried later, core features still working.
Monitoring of the vendor from your side (error rate, latency), not only their status page.
A runbook: who contacts the vendor, when to switch to a fallback, how to tell customers.
Afterwards: compare their real uptime with the SLA and revisit the decision if needed.
followups: What does an SLA credit actually give you?
How do you test the fallback path?

one: Growing other engineers and handing over meaningful work, so the team's output does not depend on you.
an: A good coach does not play every position; they make each player better and trust them on the field.
how: Delegate outcomes, not tasks: "make search fast enough for the 50k catalogue" rather than "add an index on column X". Agree on check-in points.
Match challenge to skill: stretch, not drown. Pair on the hard parts, then let go.
Ask questions before giving answers ("what options did you consider?"). Give specific, timely feedback; praise in public, correct in private.
Your output as a lead = the team's output. Being the bottleneck on every decision is a failure mode, not a badge.
why: The jump from senior to lead is mostly this: impact through others.
trade: Delegating feels slower at first. It is an investment that compounds.

myth.m: It is faster if I just do it myself.
myth.r: Faster this week. Next month you are still the only one who can, and the team is waiting on you.

q.s: You review every PR and approve every design yourself. Velocity drops as the team grows. Best change?
o: Work longer hours
Grow other reviewers and decision-makers, define guidelines, and step back to the high-risk calls
Hire fewer people
Stop reviews
q.e: Scale yourself through people and written standards.

more: Delegation levels (Management 3.0's seven: tell, sell, consult, agree, advise, inquire, delegate)
Giving specific feedback (SBI: situation, behaviour, impact)
lab: Pair with a less experienced developer for one hour on a real task; let them drive the whole time and only ask questions. Afterwards, write down which questions helped most.
docs: Lara Hogan: Resources for managers and leads
Management 3.0: Delegation Poker and the Delegation Board

plain: As you become senior and lead, your value shifts from what you build to what the team builds. Mentoring helps people grow; delegation gives them real ownership. Both feel slower at first and pay off quickly.
bridge: Think of the best senior you worked with: they probably asked you questions instead of giving answers, and trusted you with something slightly too big for you. That is the skill.

walk.title: Delegating a feature well
steps: Instead of a task (“add an index to the orders table”), give an outcome: “the orders page must load under 500ms for our largest customer”.
Agree on check-ins: a 15-minute chat after they investigate, and before they ship.
At the first check-in, ask: “What did you find? What options do you see?” Guide with questions.
They find the N+1 problem and an index issue. They fix it and present the before/after numbers at the team meeting.
Next time, they own similar problems alone. Your time goes to the next harder problem.

terms: Giving someone ownership of an outcome.
Helping someone grow through guidance and feedback.
Work slightly beyond someone's current level.
How many people would need to leave before knowledge is lost.
insights: Test your delegation by being unavailable for a day: whatever stops is what you have not handed over yet.
Quietly redoing someone's work undoes months of delegation; give feedback and let them fix it.
Sponsorship matters as much as mentoring: put people's work in front of those who decide promotions.

prod.summary: In real teams, mentoring and delegation show up as concrete habits: regular 1:1s, outcome-based tasks with agreed check-ins, pairing on the hard parts, and handing over ownership of whole areas (on-call, a service, a review area). Leads measure success by what happens when they are away: decisions still get made, PRs still get reviewed, and incidents still get handled.
checklist: Each person has a stretch goal you both know about, and work that serves it.
Delegated work states the outcome, the constraints, the deadline, and the decision level (“decide and tell me” vs “propose, I decide”).
Check-ins are agreed up front (after investigation, before shipping), not random interruptions.
You ask questions before giving answers, and let people make recoverable mistakes.
Feedback is specific and timely (within a day or two), using situation, behaviour, impact.
Credit is given publicly to the person who did the work, in demos, release notes and promotion discussions.
Bus factor check: for each critical system, at least two people can deploy, debug and be on-call for it.
numbers: Jurgen Appelo's Management 3.0 delegation board defines seven levels: tell, sell, consult, agree, advise, inquire, delegate.
Many leads run 30-minute 1:1s weekly or every two weeks; the time belongs to the report, not to status updates.
Situation-Behaviour-Impact (SBI) is a feedback model from the Center for Creative Leadership: describe the situation, the observable behaviour, and its impact.
failures: The lead goes on a two-week holiday and three PRs, one design decision and a production incident all wait for them.
All decisions and knowledge go through one person. Write down decision rules, name owners per area, rotate on-call, and practise by being “unavailable” for a day before the holiday.
A delegated feature comes back after 3 weeks, technically fine but solving the wrong problem.
The task was handed over without the outcome and constraints, and with no check-in. Delegate the goal and success criteria, and agree a check-in after the first 1–2 days of investigation.
A mid-level engineer quits, saying in the exit interview “I was never given anything interesting.”
The lead kept the hard, visible work and delegated only small tickets. Give stretch work with support (pairing, check-ins), and make sure their work is visible to the people who decide promotions.
Delegated work is quietly redone by the lead the night before release.
Low trust and unclear quality bar. Agree the bar in advance, review together, and accept solutions that are different but correct. Redoing work teaches people their ownership is not real.

qs.s: A junior asks you in chat “should I use a join or two queries here?” for the third time this week. What is the most growth-oriented reply?
o: Send the correct answer immediately to save time
Tell them to search online
Ask what options they see and what they would measure, then guide them to check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on real data
Take the task and do it yourself
qs.e: Questions plus a way to verify build judgement they can reuse. Giving the answer creates dependence; “search online” gives no guidance; taking the task removes the learning entirely.

qs.s: You delegate “make the search page fast enough for our largest customer.” What is the most important thing to agree before they start?
o: The exact database index they should add
The success criterion (e.g. p95 under 500 ms with that customer's data), constraints, deadline, and when you will check in
Which editor they should use
That they must not ask you any questions
qs.e: Outcome delegation needs a clear target and check-ins. Prescribing the index turns it back into a task; tools are irrelevant; banning questions removes support.

qs.s: A senior on your team delivers well but rarely shares knowledge; only they understand the billing service. What is the best lead action?
o: Ask them to mentor a teammate who pairs on the next billing change and joins the billing on-call, with the knowledge transfer as an explicit goal
Leave it, since the billing service works
Ask them to write a 50-page document in their free time
Move them off billing immediately
qs.e: Pairing on real work and sharing on-call transfers knowledge that docs alone do not, and making it an explicit goal gives credit for it. Ignoring it keeps a bus factor of one; a huge doc is unlikely to be written or read; moving them abruptly loses the knowledge.

qs.s: Your team uses a delegation board. For “choose libraries for a new service”, the level is Advise. An engineer asks what that means for them. What is the correct answer?

code.title: Delegation board (Management 3.0 levels)
code.src:
Decision area                   Level
--------------------------------------------
Production DB schema changes    3 Consult
Choose libraries for a service  5 Advise
On-call rota                    6 Inquire
Code style rules                7 Delegate

1 Tell  2 Sell  3 Consult  4 Agree
5 Advise  6 Inquire  7 Delegate

o: The lead decides, after asking the engineer for input
The lead and the engineer must agree together
The engineer decides alone and does not need to tell anyone
The engineer decides; the lead may give advice first, but the decision is theirs
qs.e: At level 5 (Advise) the team decides and the lead tries to influence. Asking for input and then deciding yourself is level 3 (Consult). Deciding together is level 4 (Agree). Deciding with no influence is level 7. Writing the level down prevents “I thought it was my call” conflicts.

qs.s: You drafted this feedback for an engineer. Which rewrite follows the SBI model (situation, behaviour, impact)?

code.title: Draft feedback
code.src:
You are careless with releases and you don't care
about the team.

o: “You need to be more careful in general.”
“Great job overall, but releases could be better, but keep it up!”

“In Tuesday's release (situation), the migration ran without the dry run from our checklist (behaviour). The orders table was locked for 6 minutes and support got 40 tickets (impact). Can we talk about what made skipping it feel OK?”
“Other people have said you are careless.”
qs.e: SBI names a specific moment, an observable action (what a camera would see), and its effect, without judging character. Then a question opens a conversation. The “sandwich” version hides the message; vague or second-hand criticism makes people defensive and gives them nothing to change.

qs.s: A mid-level engineer has shipped CRUD features well for a year. Which next assignment is the best stretch?
o: More CRUD features, because they are good at it
Own the design and rollout of a medium-size feature with one unknown (a new third-party API), with a design review and two agreed check-ins
Lead the full rewrite of the billing system alone
Nothing new until their next performance review
qs.e: A stretch is slightly beyond current skill, with support. One unknown plus check-ins grows design and risk skills while keeping failure recoverable. More of the same stalls growth; a solo billing rewrite risks drowning them and the business.

qs.s: You run this command on the billing service. What does it tell you, and what should you do?

code.title: Commit authors on billing, last 12 months
code.src:
git shortlog -sn --since="12 months ago" -- services/billing
#   412  Aziz
#    11  Kamola
#     6  Timur

o: The bus factor is effectively one. Have Aziz pair with Kamola on the next billing changes, rotate billing on-call, and set knowledge transfer as an explicit goal for both
Aziz is the most productive engineer, so give him more billing work
Kamola and Timur are underperforming and need a warning
Nothing; commit counts say nothing about knowledge
qs.e: Commit counts are a rough signal, but 96% from one person strongly suggests only Aziz can change billing safely. That is a risk for holidays, illness and resignation. Using commit counts to judge individual performance is a misuse of the data; ignoring the signal leaves the risk in place.

interview.q: How do you delegate work without losing quality?
answer: Delegate the outcome and the success criteria, not the steps (“p95 under 500 ms for our largest customer”).
State the decision level clearly: “decide and tell me” vs “propose, I decide”.
Agree check-ins up front: after investigation and before shipping.
Agree the quality bar in advance (tests, review, rollout), then accept different-but-correct solutions.
Do not redo delegated work; if it falls short, fix it together and adjust how you delegate next time.
followups: What do you never delegate?
How do you delegate to someone more senior than you?

interview.q: Tell me how you have helped an engineer grow.
answer: Start with their goal (for example, to become senior) and what they lack, compared to a career ladder.
Pick real work that gives that experience: a stretch assignment with support.
Teach with questions, pair on the hard parts, then step back.
Give specific, timely feedback (SBI), positive and corrective.
Make their work visible to the people who decide promotions (sponsorship), and measure growth by what they can now do alone.
followups: What is the difference between mentoring and sponsorship?
How do you handle someone who does not want to grow?

interview.q: How do you run 1:1s with the engineers you lead?
answer: Regular and protected: for example 30 minutes weekly or every two weeks; rarely cancelled.
The time belongs to them; status updates go in writing elsewhere.
Cover growth, blockers, feedback both ways, and how they feel about the work.
Keep short notes and follow up on what you promised.
Watch for signals: someone who stops raising problems may be about to leave.
followups: What do you do when 1:1s feel empty?
How do you ask for feedback about yourself?

diagrams.title: Delegation decision tree
diagrams.src:
flowchart TD A["Work you could do yourself"] --> B{"Can someone do it
with some stretch?"} B -- "no, too big" --> C["Pair on the hard part,
delegate a slice"] B -- yes --> D{"Mistakes easy
to recover from?"} D -- yes --> E["Delegate the outcome:
decide and tell me"] D -- no --> F["Delegate the outcome:
propose, I decide"] C --> G["Agree check-ins: after
investigating, before shipping"] E --> G F --> G G --> H["Guide with questions,
do not take it back"] H --> I["Public credit to them"]
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the risk of the work changes the decision level, not whether you delegate. Even the riskiest work goes to someone else with a “propose, I decide” level and agreed check-ins.

codeCheck.detail: The git shortlog command ran on a scratch repo and counted only commits under services/billing.

videos.why: Four mentorship concepts from Google engineers.

videos.t: Mentoring Junior Engineers @ Slack HQ – Carly Robinson | The Lead Developer UK 2017
videos.why: Conference talk on mentoring junior engineers at Slack.

one: Choosing the work with the best value for its cost and risk, and explicitly declining or deferring the rest.
an: A packing list for a small backpack. Everything is useful; only some of it fits.
how: Frameworks are aids: value vs effort, RICE (reach, impact, confidence, effort), cost of delay. The conversation matters more than the score.
Balance feature work, reliability, security and debt explicitly (e.g. a fixed share of capacity), instead of letting the loudest request win.
"No" is often "not now" with a reason and a trade: "if we do this, X slips two weeks."
why: Teams fail more from doing too many things half-way than from doing the wrong thing fully.
trade: Priorities change; revisit them on a cadence, not every day.

myth.m: A good team can do everything that is asked.
myth.r: Every yes is a no to something else. Making that visible is the lead's job.

q.s: Sales wants a custom feature for one prospect mid-sprint. Best lead response?
o: Drop everything
Make the trade-off explicit (what slips, by how much) and let the right owner decide
Refuse without discussion
Build it secretly at night
q.e: Surface cost and trade-offs; decisions belong with whoever owns the priority.

lab: Score your current backlog's top 10 items with RICE in a spreadsheet. Note where the score disagrees with your gut and why.

plain:
There is always more work than time. Prioritisation means choosing the work with the most value for its cost and risk, and clearly saying “not now” to the rest.

Leads also make sure reliability, security and tech debt get a share, not only new features.
bridge: Your backlog probably has 80 items marked “high priority”. When everything is high priority, nothing is. The job is to order them honestly.

walk.title: A request in the middle of a sprint
steps: Sales asks for a custom export for one big prospect, “by Friday”.
You estimate: 3 days. It would delay the payment retry fix, which affects 2% of all payments.
You write to sales and the product manager: “We can do the export by Friday if the payment fix moves one week. That fix recovers about $4k/month. Which do you prefer?”
They decide the payment fix stays; the export ships the week after, and sales tells the prospect.
You did not just say yes or no. You made the trade-off visible and let the owners decide.

terms: Ordering work by value, cost and risk.
What you give up by choosing something else.
A scoring method: Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort.
Fixed shares of time for features, reliability, debt.
insights: “Not now, because X” is far better received than a silent no or a reluctant yes.
Track interrupts for one sprint before arguing about them; real numbers end the debate.
Plan with less than 100% capacity. Support and interrupts always take a share, so plan for it openly.

prod.summary: In real teams prioritisation happens every week, under pressure from sales, support, leadership and incidents. Seniors make the trade-off visible in writing (what slips if we say yes), protect a fixed share of capacity for reliability and debt, and make sure the person who owns the priority makes the call. Scoring frameworks help start the conversation, but the conversation decides.
checklist: One ordered list, not a pile of “P1” items; if two things are equally first, pick one.
Each item has a rough value (users, revenue, risk reduced) and a rough cost, even if both are ranges.
Capacity for reliability, security and debt is reserved (for example 20%), not negotiated item by item.
Interrupts (urgent requests, incidents) are tracked, so their real cost is visible.
Every “yes” states what moves: “if we do X now, Y slips 2 weeks”.
Decisions and who made them are written down where the requesters can see them.
The list is reviewed on a cadence (weekly or per sprint), not reshuffled daily.
numbers: Intercom's RICE: score = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort; Impact uses 3 / 2 / 1 / 0.5 / 0.25, Confidence 100% / 80% / 50%, and Effort is in person-months.
Cost of delay ÷ duration (CD3, from Don Reinertsen's work) ranks items by how much value you lose per week of waiting, divided by how long they take.
Google's SRE book describes error budgets: when a service has used up its budget for unreliability, the team pauses feature launches and focuses on reliability.
failures: The sprint started with 10 items and ended with 3 done and 8 “in progress”, including 4 new urgent requests.
No limit on work in progress and no gate for interrupts. Track interrupts, set a WIP limit, and route new requests through one owner who decides what they replace.
The team has not touched the flaky deploy pipeline in 6 months; deploys now fail 1 in 5 times and everyone loses hours.
Reliability work always loses to features when compared one at a time. Reserve fixed capacity, and quantify it: “5 hours/week lost by 8 engineers” is a business number.
The CEO's idea in the hallway becomes the team's top priority without anyone checking what it replaces.
Priority is set by who is loudest. Reply in writing with the trade-off and ask the product owner to decide; show what moves on the roadmap.
The RICE spreadsheet ranks a tiny UI tweak above a security fix.

Treating the score as the decision. Risk and compliance work rarely fit RICE. Use the score as input, keep a separate lane for must-do work (security, legal), and discuss when the score disagrees with judgement.

code.title: RICE as a conversation starter (Intercom scale)
code.src:
Item                  Reach/qtr  Impact  Conf.  Effort(pm)  RICE
Saved searches            8,000     1      80%      2      3,200
Bulk CSV import             600     2      80%      1        960
Payment retry fix        12,000     0.5   100%      0.5   12,000
Dark mode                20,000     0.25   50%      1      2,500

RICE = Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort
  payment retry: 12,000 x 0.5 x 1.0 / 0.5 = 12,000
  saved search:   8,000 x 1   x 0.8 / 2   =  3,200

Not scored (separate must-do lane):
  - TLS certificate automation (outage risk)
  - Postgres 14 upgrade: community support ends 2026-11-12
code.note: Small effort with wide reach wins easily. The must-do lane keeps security and end-of-life work from being out-scored by features.

qs.s: Using RICE (Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort): Item A reaches 2,000 users, impact 2, confidence 50%, effort 1 person-month. Item B reaches 500 users, impact 3, confidence 100%, effort 0.5 person-months. Which scores higher?
o: They are equal
qs.e: A = 2,000 × 2 × 0.5 ÷ 1 = 2,000. B = 500 × 3 × 1.0 ÷ 0.5 = 3,000. The smaller effort and full confidence beat A's bigger reach. Forgetting the confidence factor gives 4,000 for A.

qs.s: Engineers want 3 weeks to fix flaky tests; product wants features. How do you make the strongest case?
o: Quantify it: “CI reruns cost ~6 engineer-hours a week and delayed 4 releases last month; 3 weeks of work pays back in about a quarter”
“Flaky tests are bad practice”
Fix the tests secretly inside feature tickets
Ask the CTO to order it
qs.e: Time and money lost are business terms the product owner can weigh against features. Opinions do not win prioritisation; hidden work destroys estimates and trust; escalating first skips the owner.

qs.s: Your team reserves 20% capacity for reliability and debt. A big customer escalation arrives and leadership asks to use that 20% for features “just this quarter”. What is the best reply?
o: Agree; reliability can wait
Refuse completely
Agree silently and keep doing reliability work anyway
Explain what that 20% is fixing and the risk of pausing it (e.g. the deploy failure rate), offer a time-boxed exception with a date to restore it, and let the owner decide in writing
qs.e: Make the trade-off and risk visible, offer a bounded option, and let the right person decide on the record. A silent yes or a hidden refusal breaks trust; a flat no ignores a real business need.

qs.s: A product manager shares this RICE sheet. What is wrong?

code.title: Backlog scoring (Intercom RICE)
code.src:
Item            Reach  Impact  Conf.  Effort(pm)  Score
Bulk invite      1,000    2      50%      1        2,000
Audit log          300    3      80%      2          360
Slack alerts     4,000    1     100%      2        2,000

o: Bulk invite's score ignores confidence: 1,000 × 2 × 0.5 ÷ 1 = 1,000, not 2,000, so Slack alerts ranks above it
Audit log is wrong: it should be 1,200
Effort should be multiplied, not divided
Nothing; all scores are correct
qs.e: Bulk invite: 1,000 × 2 × 0.5 ÷ 1 = 1,000. Audit log: 300 × 3 × 0.8 ÷ 2 = 360 (correct). Slack alerts: 4,000 × 1 × 1.0 ÷ 2 = 2,000 (correct). Forgetting the confidence factor is the most common RICE error, and it rewards uncertain ideas.

qs.s: Two items, one team, can do only one at a time. A loses $10k/week of value while it waits and takes 5 weeks. B loses $4k/week and takes 1 week. Using cost of delay divided by duration (CD3), which goes first?
o: A, because its cost of delay is higher
B: CD3 for B = 4 ÷ 1 = 4, for A = 10 ÷ 5 = 2. Doing B first delays A by 1 week ($10k); doing A first delays B by 5 weeks ($20k)
A, because it is the bigger project
It does not matter; total work is the same
qs.e: The order changes how much value you lose while items wait. Doing the short, valuable item first costs $10k of delay instead of $20k. Looking only at cost of delay (A is bigger) ignores how long it blocks everything else.

qs.s: Your team tracked interrupts for one sprint. What is the best response?

code.title: Interrupt log, sprint 41 (5 engineers, 10 days)
code.src:
Support escalations ........ 61 h
Urgent sales requests ...... 34 h
Production incidents ....... 29 h
Ad-hoc data pulls .......... 16 h
----------------------------------
Total ...................... 140 h  (about 35% of capacity)

o: Ask engineers to ignore interrupts until the sprint ends
Plan the next sprint at full capacity and work harder
Plan with about 65% capacity, rotate one “interrupt duty” engineer so the others stay focused, and attack the biggest source (for example, self-service data pulls and better support docs)
Stop accepting incidents during sprints
qs.e: The data shows a third of the team's time is not plannable today. Planning honestly, shielding the rest of the team, and reducing the largest source is how you get capacity back. Ignoring incidents or support is not an option for a production team; planning at 100% guarantees missed commitments.

qs.s: Your service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. This month it has already been down 50 minutes, and a big feature launch is planned for tomorrow. What does an error-budget policy suggest?
o: Launch; 50 minutes is small
Launch, then raise the SLO to 99.99% next month
Cancel the feature permanently
The budget is about 43 minutes (0.1% of 43,200 minutes) and it is spent, so pause risky launches and focus on reliability until the service is back within budget
qs.e: 30 days × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes; 0.1% = 43.2 minutes allowed. 50 minutes is over budget. The error-budget policy (described in Google's SRE books) turns a reliability vs features argument into an agreed rule. Pausing is not cancelling; the launch continues once reliability recovers.

interview.q: How do you handle more requests than your team can do?
answer: Keep one ordered list, owned by one person (usually the product owner), not several piles of “P1”.
Give each item a rough value and cost; use RICE or cost of delay to start the conversation, not to end it.
Every new yes states what moves: “if we do X now, Y slips two weeks”.
Reserve capacity for reliability, security and debt, and keep a separate lane for must-do work (security fixes, end-of-life upgrades).
Write decisions down where requesters can see them, and review the order on a cadence.
followups: What do you say to an executive who wants their item first?
How do you limit work in progress?

interview.q: How do you get time for tech debt or reliability work?
answer: Translate it into business terms: hours lost per week, incidents, delayed releases, risk to revenue or contracts.
Agree a standing share of capacity (for example around 20%) instead of arguing item by item.
Pick debt that slows current roadmap work, so the payback is visible.
Use error budgets or SLOs as an agreed trigger for reliability work.
Report the results after: “deploy failures dropped from 1 in 5 to 1 in 30”.
followups: What if leadership takes the capacity away “just this quarter”?
How do you choose which debt to pay first?

interview.q: Tell me about a time you said no to a stakeholder.
answer: Describe the request and why it mattered to them; show you understood their goal.
Explain the trade-off you made visible (what it would displace and the cost).
Offer an alternative: “not now”, a smaller version, or a date.
Let the right owner decide, and write it down.
Say what happened afterwards and what you learned about the relationship.
followups: What if they went over your head?
Have you ever said yes and regretted it?

diagrams.title: Handling an urgent request
diagrams.src:
flowchart TD A["New urgent request"] --> B{"Must-do lane?
security, legal, incident"} B -- yes --> C["Do it, report what slipped"] B -- no --> D["Estimate cost and value"] D --> E["Find what it would push out"] E --> F["Write the trade-off:
if X now, Y slips 1 week"] F --> G["Priority owner decides"] G --> H["Decision written where
requesters can see it"] C --> H
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the lead never answers a plain yes or no. In the walk-through, the custom export becomes “export by Friday means the payment fix slips a week”, and the product manager decides.

codeCheck.detail: A RICE table, not code. All four scores (3,200 / 960 / 12,000 / 2,500) re-computed in Node; Postgres 14 end of life 2026-11-12 matches the PostgreSQL versioning policy.

videos.t: How to do Prioritization as a Software Engineer (From L8 SWE at Microsoft)
videos.why: How a principal engineer prioritises their work.

one: Translating technical reality into business terms (time, money, risk, customers) and back.
an: An interpreter at a negotiation. Both sides are smart; they just speak different languages.
how: Lead with the conclusion and the ask, then the reasoning ("We need 2 weeks for X, otherwise we risk Y").
Quantify: users affected, revenue at risk, hours saved. Avoid jargon or define it in one line.
Status updates: what is done, what is next, risks and what you need. Red/amber/green only if it reflects reality.
Write things down: decisions in a shared channel or doc beat hallway agreements.
why: Most technical work that fails to get prioritised fails because it was explained in engineering terms to people who decide in business terms.
trade: Simplifying is not hiding. Keep uncertainty visible.

myth.r: Invisible work gets cut. Making impact visible is part of the job.

q.s: How should you explain the need to upgrade an end-of-life database version to a CEO?
o: "Postgres 12 is EOL and lacks the newer planner features"
"Our database stops getting security fixes in March; a breach or outage would hit customers and contracts. Two weeks of work removes that risk."
Do not explain
Send the release notes
q.e: Risk, impact, cost, in their terms.

lab: Rewrite a recent technical message you sent (Slack, PR description) for a non-technical reader: conclusion first, impact in money/time/users, one clear ask, under 120 words.
docs: Gergely Orosz: How can I work better with my product manager, as an engineering lead?

plain: Most decisions about technical work are made by people who are not engineers. Explaining in their terms (time, money, risk, customers) is what gets important work approved. Start with the conclusion and the request, then give the reasoning.
bridge: Compare “we need to upgrade Postgres 12” with “our database stops receiving security fixes in March; two weeks of work removes that risk”. Same work; only the second gets a yes.

walk.title: A status update a manager actually reads
steps: Bad: three paragraphs about refactoring the webhook handler and race conditions.
Good, first line: “Payments project: on track for 15 Nov, one risk.”
Second: “Done: card payments live for 10% of users, 0 failures in 3 days.”
Third: “Risk: the provider's refund API is unreliable. Option A: manual refunds for 2 weeks. Option B: delay launch 1 week. I recommend A.”
Fourth: “Need from you: a decision on A or B by Thursday.”

terms: Anyone affected by or deciding about the work.
Bottom line up front: conclusion first.
The specific thing you need from the reader.
A regular short summary of progress, risks and needs.
insights: Numbers (users affected, money, hours) persuade more than technical detail.
Use the same update format every week (status, done, next, risks, asks); readers learn where to look.
A risk that may move a date gets a direct message to the decider as well as the shared update, not only a line in a weekly doc.

prod.summary: In real teams, most communication with non-engineers is written: weekly status updates, incident summaries, launch notes and decision requests. Seniors write with the conclusion first, use the reader's units (customers, money, dates, risk), keep uncertainty visible, and always state the ask with a deadline. Good communication is also early: a risk raised in week 2 is a choice, the same risk in week 6 is a crisis.
checklist: First line: status and the bottom line (“On track for 15 Nov, one risk needs a decision”).
Each risk has impact in business units, probability, options and your recommendation.
One clear ask, with who and by when (“Decision on A or B from Dilnoza by Thursday”).
Green / amber / red reflects reality; amber is raised early, not hidden until it turns red.
Jargon is removed or defined in one line; numbers have units and are rounded.
The same message goes to everyone in one shared place (channel, doc), so there are no different versions of the truth.
After an incident, a customer-facing summary is ready: what happened, who was affected, what we changed.
numbers: PostgreSQL supports each major version for 5 years; for example PostgreSQL 14 receives its final release on 12 November 2026, PostgreSQL 13 ended on 13 November 2025.
BLUF (bottom line up front) comes from US military writing guidance: state the conclusion and the request in the first sentences.
failures: Leadership learns about a 4-week delay in the launch meeting, from a slide that was green last week.
The status colour reflected hope, not data, and the risk was not raised early. Re-forecast weekly from slices done, turn amber as soon as a risk could move the date, and bring options.
A request for two weeks to upgrade the database is rejected as “technical cleanup”.

It was explained in engineering terms. Reframe as risk and cost: “Our database version stops getting security fixes on 12 November; an unpatched breach would affect all 40k customers and our bank contract. Two weeks removes that risk.”
Sales and support tell customers different launch dates.
Updates were sent in private messages to different people. Publish one status in a shared channel or doc, and point everyone to it.
A stakeholder approves a plan, then says weeks later “I never agreed to cutting refunds.”
The decision was made verbally. Write the decision, options considered and the decider in a short message right after the meeting, and ask for a reply.

code.title: A weekly status update that gets read
code.src:
Payments v2 - week 4 of 7 - AMBER (date at risk, decision needed)

Bottom line: on track for Thu 29 Oct only if we ship without refunds.

Done this week:
- Card payments live for 10% of users; 2,140 payments, 0 failures.

Risk:
- The provider's refund API fails ~5% of calls in testing.
  Impact: customers waiting days for refunds; support load.

Options:
  A. Launch Thu 29 Oct; support does refunds manually for ~2 weeks
     (est. 30 refunds/week, ~1 hour/day of support time).
  B. Delay launch to Thu 5 Nov and ship automatic refunds.
Recommendation: A.

Ask: decision on A or B from Dilnoza (Product) by Thu 8 Oct.
Next week: rollout to 50%, reconciliation report.
code.note: Status, bottom line, impact in business terms, options with a recommendation, and one named ask with a date. Technical detail lives in a linked doc.

qs.s: During an outage, the head of sales asks in the incident channel “what's happening?”. Which reply is best?
o: “Investigating a connection-pool exhaustion on the primary after the 14:02 deploy, checking pgbouncer logs”
No reply until the incident is fixed
“Checkout is failing for about 30% of customers since 14:05. We have rolled back the likely cause and expect recovery within 20 minutes. Next update at 14:45.”
“Everything will be fine soon”
qs.e: Impact in their terms, what is being done, an estimate, and when the next update comes. Technical detail is for engineers; silence and vague reassurance both reduce trust.

qs.s: A product manager asks if a feature can ship by Friday. You think there is a 50% chance. What is the most useful answer?
o: “About 50/50. The risk is the export API's rate limit; I will know Wednesday. If it is a problem, we can ship without bulk export on Friday and add it next week.”
“Yes”, to keep them happy
“No”, to be safe
“It depends”
qs.e: Honest probability, the specific risk, when you will know more, and a fallback option. A plain yes or no hides the uncertainty; “it depends” gives nothing to plan with.

qs.s: You must explain to the CFO why you want to move from a $900/month managed database to a $2,300/month one. Which argument fits the reader best?
o: “The new one has a better query planner and more IOPS”
“All modern companies use it”
“It has read replicas and point-in-time recovery”
“Last quarter we had 2 database outages costing about 9 hours of checkout downtime (~$18k in lost orders). The new plan's failover and backups cut that risk sharply for $16.8k per year.”
qs.e: The CFO decides on money and risk: lost revenue vs extra cost (12 × $1,400 = $16,800). Features and fashion are not decision criteria for them, even when they are the technical reason.

qs.s: Read this status update for leadership. What is the most important improvement?

code.title: Draft status, #leadership
code.src:
This week we refactored the webhook handler to use an
idempotency key table and moved retries to BullMQ. We also
found a race in the reconciliation job and fixed the
flaky e2e tests. Next week we continue with refunds.
Status: GREEN

o: Add more technical detail so leadership trusts the work
Change GREEN to RED to be safe
Start with the bottom line in their terms (is the launch date safe, who is affected, any risk), then any decision needed; move technical detail to a linked doc
Send it as a private message to each leader
qs.e: Leadership reads for date, risk, and decisions they must make. This update forces them to guess. Marking RED without reason is as misleading as a hopeful GREEN. Private messages create different versions of the truth.

qs.s: The product manager asks why the team wants two sprints for “refactoring the order module”. Which explanation is most likely to get a fair decision?
o: “Each new order feature takes us about twice as long as it should; the last three took 9 weeks instead of ~4, and 4 of last quarter's 7 incidents came from this module. Two sprints should cut both, so the Q1 roadmap ships about a month sooner.”
“The code is very messy and uses old patterns.”
“Every good engineering team does regular refactoring.”
“We will do it inside feature tickets so you do not need to decide.”
qs.e: Time lost, incidents and roadmap impact are things a product manager can weigh against features. “Messy” and “everyone does it” are engineering opinions. Hiding the work inside tickets breaks estimates and trust.

qs.s: An engineer wrote this update to the CFO after an incident. What is missing?

code.title: Email to CFO
code.src:
Subject: Incident on 2 Oct

On 2 Oct a misconfigured connection pool caused checkout
errors from 14:05 to 14:52. We rolled back the deploy and
increased the pool size. All systems are normal now.

o: The name of the engineer who made the mistake
The full database logs
A longer technical explanation of connection pools
Business impact (how many customers and orders failed, estimated lost revenue, any refunds or contract issues) and what changes so it does not happen again, beyond a bigger pool
qs.e: A CFO needs impact in money and customers, and confidence that the cause is fixed. Blame and raw logs do not help them decide anything, and naming a person damages a blameless culture. The update also treats a symptom (pool size) as the fix.

qs.s: Your project's status has been GREEN for 6 weeks. Today you learn the bank's sandbox will be late, which could move the launch by 2 weeks, but it is not certain yet. What do you do?
o: Stay GREEN until it is certain, to avoid panic
Switch to AMBER today, explain the risk, when you will know more, and the options if it happens
Switch to RED immediately
Mention it only in the retrospective after launch
qs.e: AMBER means “date at risk”, which is exactly this. Raising it early gives stakeholders time to plan (marketing, sales promises). Waiting for certainty turns a choice into a surprise. RED overstates a risk that is not yet confirmed.

interview.q: How do you explain a technical risk to a non-technical executive?
answer: Start with the bottom line and the ask: what you need and by when.
Use their units: customers affected, money, dates, contracts, legal risk.
Give probability and impact honestly, including uncertainty; do not hide it to sound confident.
Offer options with costs and a recommendation.
Keep it short; link the technical detail for anyone who wants it.
followups: What if they choose the option you advised against?
How do you explain uncertainty without sounding unsure?

interview.q: How do you write a status update that people actually read?
answer: First line: status colour and bottom line (“on track for 15 Nov, one risk”).
Done, next, risks (with impact and options), and one named ask with a deadline.
Colours reflect reality; turn amber as soon as the date is at risk.
Same message for everyone in one shared place.
Same structure every week, so readers know where to look.
followups: How often should you send them?
What do you do when nobody replies to your ask?

interview.q: A sales lead promised a customer a feature by a date the team never agreed to. What do you do?
answer: Talk to the sales lead privately first; understand the deal and what the customer really needs.
Give an honest range and the options: a smaller version by the date, the full feature later, or moving other work (with the cost).
Let the product owner decide, in writing, and help sales reset expectations with the customer.
Fix the process: estimates are given in writing with ranges, and dates go through one owner.
followups: What if the deal is worth a lot of money?
How do you prevent it from happening again without slowing sales?

diagrams.title: Raising a risk so it becomes a decision
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Lead
  participant PM as Product manager
  participant Org as Sales and support
  Note over Lead: Refund API is unreliable
  Lead->>PM: AMBER, one risk, options A or B, I recommend A
  Lead->>PM: Need your decision by Thursday
  PM->>Lead: Go with A, manual refunds for 2 weeks
  Lead->>PM: Written recap of decision, options, decider
  Lead->>Org: One shared update, 15 Nov date unchanged
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the risk is raised as soon as it is known, with options and a recommendation, and it ends in a written recap and one shared message, so nobody hears a different version.

videos.t: Explaining Technical Information to Non-Technical People
videos.why: Explaining technical information to non-technical people.

one: Owning outcomes end to end: understanding why, shipping, measuring, operating, and following up, without being told each step.
an: A homeowner, not a renter: you fix the leak you noticed even if no one asked, because it is your house.
how: Ask why before how. Clarify the problem and success criteria before writing code.
Close loops: after shipping, check the metrics, read the errors, talk to users or support.
Reduce ambiguity for others: write things down, propose a plan, unblock teammates.
Know when to escalate: early, with context and a recommendation.
why: Teams give big, ambiguous problems only to people who will carry them to a working result in production without supervision. Building that trust is what moves you from mid-level to senior.
trade: Ownership is not doing everything alone; it includes pulling in the right help.

myth.r: Senior = reliably turns ambiguous problems into shipped, operating outcomes, and makes others more effective while doing it.

q.s: You shipped a feature last week. What does a senior do next without being asked?
o: Move on to the next ticket
Check adoption and error metrics, follow up on issues, and share what was learned
Wait for QA reports
Refactor unrelated code
q.e: Shipping is the midpoint; the outcome is what matters.

more: Scope and ambiguity as the axes of seniority
lab: Read two public engineering career ladders and highlight every expectation you do not yet meet. Pick one to practise this month on real work.

plain: The biggest difference between a mid-level and a senior engineer is not knowing more technologies. It is ownership: taking a vague problem, figuring out what is actually needed, delivering it, checking it works in production, and following up, without someone guiding each step.
bridge: A mid-level developer closes the ticket when the PR merges. A senior opens the dashboard the next day to see if the feature works for users and is used at all.

walk.title: Same task, two levels
steps: Task: “Add CSV export to the orders page.”
Mid-level: builds the button and export, PR merged, ticket closed.
Senior: first asks who needs it and why; learns accountants need it monthly for tax, with specific columns.
Builds it as a background job (large exports would block the server), tests with the biggest customer's data, adds an error alert.
A week later checks usage and errors, finds one timezone bug, fixes it, and tells the accountants it is ready.

terms: Responsibility for the outcome, not just the task.
The size and ambiguity of problems you are trusted with.
Checking results after shipping and following up.
Raising a problem early to someone who can help.
insights: Shipping is the middle of the job, not the end.
Put a day-1 and day-7 check in your calendar when you ship; it turns closing the loop into a habit.
An alert nobody owns is now your problem once you have seen it: fix it, or give it an owner.

prod.summary: In production teams, ownership is visible in behaviour after the merge: the owner watches dashboards and error rates during rollout, reads support tickets about their feature, writes the runbook, and fixes or hands over the follow-ups. Seniors are trusted with ambiguous problems because they close loops, raise risks early with a recommendation, and leave systems easier to operate than they found them.
checklist: Before building: the problem, the user, and the success metric are written down and agreed.
Before shipping: alerts, dashboards and a rollback path exist for the new feature.
During rollout: you watch error rate, latency and the key business metric for the first hours and days.
After shipping: you check adoption, read related support tickets, and create follow-up tickets for what you learned.
Every escalation includes context, what you tried, options and a recommendation.
Things you notice outside your task (a failing cron job, a confusing doc) get fixed or turned into a ticket with an owner, not ignored.
When you hand work over, there is a written handover: state, risks, open questions, where the dashboards are.
numbers: Amazon's “Ownership” leadership principle: leaders act on behalf of the entire company, beyond their own team, and never say “that's not my job”.
Public career ladders (for example Dropbox's engineering career framework) describe seniority mostly by scope, ambiguity and impact on others, not by the number of technologies known.
A practical habit: put a calendar reminder for 1 day, 1 week and 1 month after launch to review the feature's metrics and errors.
failures: A feature shipped a month ago; nobody noticed it has a 12% error rate on mobile until a customer complained.
Ownership ended at merge. Add a launch checklist (dashboard, alert on error rate, post-launch review at day 1 and day 7) and make the author responsible for it.
An engineer spends two weeks stuck on an integration problem and mentions it only at the sprint review.
Escalation felt like failure. Agree a rule (stuck for more than a day: ask; more than three: escalate with options), and praise early escalations publicly.
A built export feature is technically perfect but accountants still email the team for CSVs, because it lacks the columns they need.
The engineer built the ticket, not the outcome. Talk to the real users before building, and check usage after launch.
A nightly job fails every night for months; everyone sees the alert and assumes someone else owns it.
No named owner. Every alert and job needs an owning team in its metadata; the lead assigns orphaned ones and removes alerts nobody acts on.

qs.s: While fixing a bug, you notice the password-reset emails link to http:// instead of https://. It is not in your ticket. What does an owner do?
o: Ignore it; it is not your task
Mention it in a hallway conversation
Fix it now if it is small and safe (or create a ticket with an owner and severity), and tell the team
Wait for the security team to find it
qs.e: Ownership means acting on problems you see, through the normal process. Ignoring it or relying on someone else to notice leaves a real security issue open; a hallway mention gets forgotten.

qs.s: You are asked to “make onboarding better”. There is no spec. What is the best first step?
o: Start redesigning the onboarding screens
Ask for a detailed spec before doing anything
Look at the onboarding funnel data and talk to support to find where users drop off, then propose a goal and a plan for agreement
Add more tooltips
qs.e: Seniors turn vague problems into clear ones using data and users, then get agreement. Building first risks solving the wrong problem; waiting for a spec gives the ambiguity back to someone else.

qs.s: You are three days into a task estimated at two days, and you have found that the third-party API does not support a field you need. What is the best escalation message?
o: “The provider API does not return the tax ID we need. Options: (1) ask their support, 2–5 days; (2) collect it from users at checkout, +2 days; (3) ship without it and backfill. I recommend 2. Can we decide today?”
“I'm blocked.”
Nothing until you find a workaround
“The estimate was wrong, the API is bad.”
qs.e: Good escalation is early, with context, options, costs and a recommendation, so the decider can act in minutes. “I'm blocked” pushes the thinking to someone else; silence wastes days; blame helps nobody.

qs.s: You launched a feature behind a flag at 10% of users this morning. What should you do?

code.title: Launch dashboard, 6 hours after rollout
code.src:
web       iOS       Android
Error rate         0.3%      0.4%      4.1%
p95 latency        310ms     340ms     1.9s
Feature used by    1,240     980       610

Alert: none (threshold set at 5%)

o: Nothing; no alert fired, so it is healthy
Stop the rollout (or turn the flag off for Android), investigate the Android errors and latency, and lower the alert threshold to something your baseline supports
Roll forward to 100% to get more data
Wait for user complaints to confirm there is a problem
qs.e: Android errors are about 10 times higher than other platforms and latency is far worse. The alert did not fire only because the threshold is too high. An owner watches the dashboard during rollout instead of trusting the alert, and uses the flag to limit damage.

qs.s: A “disk 80% full” alert on a reporting server fired 210 times last month. Nobody acted on any of them. As an engineer who cares about ownership, what is the best action?
o: Mute the channel
Raise the threshold to 95% so it fires less
Wait for the disk to fill up to prove it matters
Find or assign an owner, decide if the alert needs action (if yes: fix the cause, add a runbook; if no: delete it), and tell the team
qs.e: An alert nobody acts on trains people to ignore all alerts. Either it means something (fix the cause, give it an owner and a runbook) or it should not exist. Raising the threshold only hides the noise, and it may also hide a real future problem.

qs.s: You are moving to another team and hand over a service. What is the most important thing missing from this handover?

code.title: Handover note: notifications-service
code.src:
Repo: github.com/acme/notifications
Deploy: merge to main, CI deploys automatically
Docs: README.md
New owner: Kamola
Good luck!

o: Known risks and open issues, where the dashboards and alerts are, the on-call runbook, and a few sessions where Kamola deploys and debugs while you are still reachable
The history of every commit
A list of all the libraries used
A thank-you message to the team
qs.e: A real handover transfers the operational knowledge: what can break, how you would notice, and what to do. Repo links and the README do not contain what is in your head. Commit history and library lists are already in the repo.

qs.s: You argued for Postgres full-text search; the team decided on a managed search service. The decision is recorded. What does ownership look like now?
o: Keep raising the same objection in every meeting
Do the integration slowly, to show the decision was wrong
Commit fully to making the managed service work, and raise new evidence (cost, latency, data) through the agreed review trigger if it appears
Ask to be moved off the project
qs.e: “Disagree and commit” is part of ownership: once a decision is made with your input, you help it succeed. New facts are welcome, through the review process. Re-arguing without new evidence or working slowly damages the team and the outcome.

interview.q: What does ownership mean to you? Give an example.
answer: Responsibility for the outcome, not the ticket: understand why, deliver, check it works in production, follow up.
A concrete story: the problem, what you did beyond the ticket (talked to users, added monitoring, found a bug after launch), and the measurable result.
Ownership includes asking for help and escalating early with options.
Acting on problems outside your task through the normal process (fix or ticket with an owner).
followups: When did ownership go too far, for example doing work that was not yours to do?
How do you balance ownership with focus on your own tasks?

interview.q: You are given a vague problem with no spec. How do you approach it?
answer: Find out who has the problem and why now; look at data (funnels, tickets, logs) and talk to users or support.
Write a short problem statement with a measurable goal and non-goals, and get agreement.
Propose a plan with the smallest useful first step, and the risks.
Ship in slices, measure, and adjust.
Keep stakeholders informed in writing as the picture becomes clearer.
followups: What if the stakeholders disagree about the goal?
How do you know when to stop investigating and start building?

interview.q: Tell me about a time something you shipped broke in production.
answer: Short facts: what broke, who was affected, how you found out.
What you did in the moment: stop the damage first (rollback, flag off), then communicate.
Root cause, without blaming people; what in the process let it through.
Changes you made after: tests, alerts, review checklist, rollout steps.
What you do differently now.
followups: How did you find out, from monitoring or from users?
What would have caught it earlier?

diagrams.title: The ownership loop
diagrams.src:
flowchart TD A["Vague request"] --> B["Ask why: user, problem,
success metric"] B --> C["Build with alerts
and a rollback path"] C --> D["Merge and ship
(many stop here)"] D --> E["Watch errors, latency, usage
on day 1 and day 7"] E --> F{"Works for the
real users?"} F -- no --> G["Fix it or file a
follow-up with an owner"] G --> E F -- yes --> H["Tell the users,
write the runbook"]
diagrams.caption: What to notice: shipping sits in the middle of the loop. In the CSV export walk-through, the day-7 check finds the timezone bug, and the loop ends only when the accountants are told it is ready.
